CapitaLand-Far East Organization-Sing Holdings consortium tops Town Hall Link tender with $1.82 bil bid
article:
The Government Land Sales (GLS) tender for a white site at Town Hall Link in Jurong Lake District (JLD) closed on Nov 17, attracting two bids. A consortium comprising CapitaLand Development , Far East Organization and Sing Holdings submitted the highest offer of over $1.82 billion, or $910 psf per plot ratio (ppr).

The consortium's bid was 38.9% higher than the second bid of over $1.31 billion ($655 psf ppr) submitted by Sim Lian Group .

The 99-year leasehold site is expected to yield up to 1,200 private residential units, alongside office, retail and other commercial uses. Located within JLD, the development will help transform the area into Singapore's largest mixed-use business district outside the city centre.

The Town Hall Link site was launched for tender on July 3. Spanning 400,719 sq ft, it has a maximum gross floor area (GFA) of about 2 million sq ft.

The development must include at least 40,000 sqm (430,556 sq ft) of office space and between 20,000 sqm and 44,000 sqm of retail space. Other permitted uses include serviced apartments, hotels, recreational and community facilities.

In a joint statement, CapitaLand Development, Far East Organization and Sing Holdings say the site's scale, mixed-use potential and connectivity to Jurong East MRT interchange and the future Cross Island Line station align with their expertise in developing large integrated urban projects.

“We see an opportunity to create a vibrant live-work-play destination at JLD, as Singapore’s largest mixed-use business node outside the city centre,” the consortium says.

Limited bids for large mixed-use site

The nearly 39% gap between the two bids suggests developers differ in their assessment of the value that can be extracted from the site, says Leonard Tay, head of research at Knight Frank Singapore.

Wong Siew Ying, head of research and content at PropNex, says the two bids were not unexpected, given the substantial capital commitment required for a development of this scale.

Since 2021, the 10 GLS sites sold for at least $1 billion have attracted an average of about three bids, with two sites drawing just one bid each, she notes.

Such tenders tend to appeal to a smaller pool of well-capitalised developers and consortiums, particularly when mixed-use projects require expertise across residential, office and retail development, Wong adds.

While the site's strategic location and transport connectivity are attractive, developers would have weighed these advantages against the substantial execution risks associated with a large integrated development, says Knight Frank's Tay.

In particular, the mandatory office component poses a challenge at a time when "the popularity of suburban office facilities remains untested", he adds.

Smaller site, higher land rate

The Town Hall Link site forms part of the original 6.5ha JLD master developer site, which was launched for tender in June 2023.

When the tender closed in March 2024, it attracted two concept proposals from a single consortium comprising CapitaLand Development, City Developments Ltd (CDL) , Frasers Property , Mitsubishi Estate and Mitsui Fudosan .

However, URA decided not to award the site in September 2024, as the shortlisted proposal's bid of about $2.5 billion, or $640 psf ppr, was deemed too low.

Following the unsuccessful tender, URA scaled down the development opportunity to about half the original maximum GFA to make it more accessible to a broader pool of developers.

Mohan Sandrasegeran, head of research and data analytics at SRI, says the revised site configuration will allow developers to pursue a "more focused development strategy".

PropNex's Wong notes that the Government will also undertake more infrastructure and land preparation works for the area south of Jurong Town Hall Road, potentially reducing development costs for the successful tenderer.

The smaller site and reduced infrastructure obligations may have lowered bidders' capital commitments and development risks, supporting a higher land rate this time, she adds. However, Wong cautions that the two sites are not directly comparable.

The latest top bid of $910 psf ppr is 42.2% higher than the $640 psf ppr offered for the original master developer site in 2024.

Nevertheless, Knight Frank's Tay says it remains uncertain whether the Government will award the site, as the latest bid could still fall short of its reserve price.

However, Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia, believes the Government should award the site to kick-start JLD's development.

He considers the latest bid fair, noting that the land rate is significantly higher than that offered in 2024, despite relatively unchanged conditions in the suburban office and retail markets.

While office demand remains relatively weak, residential prices have risen significantly over the same period, Yip adds.

Potential record for white site outside Central Area

CapitaLand Development, which was part of the original five-member consortium in 2024, has now returned with Far East Organization and Sing Holdings, submitting the highest bid for the smaller Town Hall Link site.

Yip also notes that the $1.82 billion bid is likely to set a record as the highest land price by quantum for a white site outside the Central Area.

For comparison, the last white site sold in the Jurong East Planning Area was acquired for $969 million ($1,012 psf ppr) in May 2011.

The site has since been developed into Westgate, a mixed-use development comprising a seven-storey retail mall and a 20-storey Grade-A office tower linked to Jurong East MRT interchange.

Meanwhile, the white site now occupied by IOI Central Boulevard Towers in the CBD attracted seven bids when its tender closed in November 2016. IOI Properties Group secured the site for $2.57 billion ($1,689 psf ppr).

"Buyers and investors remain highly attracted to transit-oriented integrated sites," says Yip.

The Town Hall Link development will have an underground connection to the future Jurong Lake District MRT station on the Cross Island Line, as well as an elevated pedestrian bridge linking it to Jurong East MRT interchange, which serves the North-South and East-West lines and will eventually connect to the Jurong Region Line.

The site is also close to established shopping malls, including JEM , Westgate and IMM, providing future residents with convenient access to retail, dining and other amenities, says Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore.

Commercial and residential opportunities

Upon full completion, JLD is expected to accommodate 100,000 new jobs and 20,000 new homes, strengthening its position as a major employment and residential hub in western Singapore.

The substantial office component at Town Hall Link will support the area's development as a decentralised commercial hub, while its future office population could drive demand for homes and retail amenities within the integrated development.

According to Huttons Data Analytics, Singapore's office supply pipeline is projected to peak in 2028 before tapering off over the following three years, potentially reducing future supply risks for developers.

Other major projects planned for JLD include the new Science Centre Singapore, slated to open by end-2027, and Jurong Gateway Hub, an integrated development expected to be completed in 2029.

Residential prices could average above $2,800 psf

The Town Hall Link site is also close to two 99-year leasehold private residential developments in Jurong Gateway: the 738-unit J Gateway , launched in June 2013, and the 368-unit J'den , launched a decade later in November 2023.

J Gateway was nearly sold out on its first day of launch, with units sold in the first month averaging $1,466 psf, based on caveats lodged. Completed in 2016, the development has seen 26 resale transactions so far this year, averaging $2,092 psf.

Meanwhile, J'den sold 88% of its units on its launch weekend at an average price of $2,451 psf. The nine units sold so far this year have averaged $2,545 psf, bringing total sales at the project to 98.5%, based on caveats lodged.

The most recent GLS site awarded in the wider Jurong area was at Lakeside Drive, which CDL secured in June 2025 for $607 million, or $1,132 psf ppr.

The site is being developed into the 570-unit Lucerne Grand, which was launched on the first weekend of October 2026. The project saw 350 units (61.4%) sold during its launch weekend at an average price of $2,480 psf.

Based on caveats lodged to date, Lucerne Grand is 72.6% sold at an average price of $2,489 psf.

PropNex's Wong expects the residential component of the Town Hall Link development to attract healthy interest from HDB upgraders in the west and buyers drawn to its connectivity and proximity to schools.

She estimates that new apartments at the development could achieve an average selling price above $2,800 psf, supported by its integrated mixed-use concept, future access to four MRT lines and JLD's ongoing transformation.

title: Executive condo prices likely to remain stable, developers may sell around 1,800 new units in 2027: Huttons
article:
Prices of executive condos (ECs), a hybrid public-private housing class, are likely to hold steady next year while up to 1,995 new units from five projects could be launched for sale, according to Huttons Asia’s forecasts.

Housing developers may also sell between 1,500 and 1,800 EC units in 2027.

The real estate agency noted a potential surge in demand in the coming year from both first- and second-time buyers who are keen to avoid the tighter EC policies.

The new restrictions on the EC market — which include a longer minimum occupation period (MOP) and the removal of the deferred payment scheme (DPS) — as well as the higher income ceiling of $18,000 are expected to apply to projects launched from 2028 onwards.

Explore comprehensive data about all ECs , including the average profit at 5 and 10 years

In the meantime, the five upcoming launches slated for 2027 will remain under the previous policy framework.

“Furthermore, the number of HDB flats fulfilling their five-year MOP will increase by 40.5% y-o-y in 2027 to 18,939 units, significantly increasing the available pool of second-time buyers,” said Huttons on Nov 17.

It added that although higher interest rates are likely in 2027, buyers of new EC units can still opt for DPS then to manage their mortgage instalments.

Forecast launches and sales of EC projects in 2026 and 2027:

Upcoming launches next year include the 430-unit Wynwood Grand and 570-unit Clovelle of Woodlands, both situated along Woodlands Drive 17; the 300-unit Solano Grand on Senja Close; the 265-unit Fablewoode Residences on Sembawang Road; and the 452-unit Miltonia Close in Yishun.

In 2026, average prices for new EC projects climbed past the $1,900 psf benchmark. This came after they had exceeded $1,700 psf in 2025.

Two EC developments were launched this year: Coastal Cabana in January and Rivelle Tampines in March. In total, 1,320 new EC units were offered for sale, similar to 2025.

Huttons on Nov 17 noted that Coastal Cabana has sold more than 85% of its homes at a median price of $1,800 psf. It is the first EC project in 12 years in Jalan Loyang Besar and also features sea views.

Meanwhile, Rivelle Tampines has moved almost 98% of its units at a median price of $1,934 psf. Likely the last EC project in the east in 2026 and 2027, it is next to a mixed-use development linked to Tampines West MRT Station.

Overall, Huttons estimated that a total of 1,500 new EC units would be sold for the whole of this year, slightly below 2025’s sales volume of 1,630 units.

“Extending a trend since 2023 of sales outpacing new launches, these figures underscore strong market demand for affordable private housing,” Huttons wrote.

In particular, new EC units continue to have a “strong pricing advantage” over new private non-landed homes situated in the Outside Central Region (OCR) or suburbs, the agency added.

The median price quantum for ECs this year stood at $1.826 million, roughly 26% lower than that of OCR private condos. In terms of psf prices, the median for ECs was $1,846 psf, which represents a 21% discount.

title: Former London barracks site to become 120 luxury homes at St John's Wood Square, priced from GBP5.25 mil
article:
Savills Singapore is introducing St John’s Wood Square, a luxury residential development on the site of the former St John’s Wood Barracks in northwest London, to buyers in Singapore. Prices start from GBP5.25 million (about $9 million) for a two-bedroom residence, the firm said in a Nov 17 release.

The development will have 120 residences, including single-level apartments, duplexes, penthouses and townhouses. The homes have an average size of over 3,260 sq ft.

Sales launched in October, and completion is phased from spring 2028 to 1Q2029.

The project’s site was previously used as military barracks for the King’s Troop and the Royal Horse Artillery. In 2012, late Malaysian-born entrepreneur Ananda Krishnan purchased the 5.5 acre (2.2ha) plot for GBP250 million.

Looking to invest in overseas properties ? Explore projects available for sale around the world

According to Savills, the development is now led by George Iacobescu, the project’s executive chairman and former chairman and CEO of Canary Wharf Group.

The project will include 2.6 acres of landscaped gardens and about 40,000 sq ft of private residents’ amenities. The centrepiece is The Riding Club, a members’ club in the restored Riding School, a Grade II-listed building built in 1825.

Amenities include a 20m swimming pool, spa and wellness facilities, sports courts, private dining areas, a cinema and children’s play spaces.

The development is located near The Regent’s Park, Primrose Hill, Marylebone and London’s West End. The St John’s Wood area is known for its green spaces, independent shops and proximity to international schools.

Iacobescu said the aim was to create “residences that respect and complement their surroundings, while delivering an unrivalled level of craftsmanship, comfort and quality”.

Noting that Krishnan envisioned “a meaningful long-term retention” of the project, he added that the developer will oversee the estate’s ongoing operation as its “long-term custodians”.

Adrian Lim, head of international residential sales at Savills Singapore, said London continues to appeal to Singapore-based buyers looking for established neighbourhoods with long-term value.

He said the project offers “a rare combination of heritage, exclusivity and contemporary luxury”.

title: Hotel investments may reach US$1.3 bil in Singapore this year as regional momentum defies headwinds: JLL
article:
In Singapore, hotel investment deals have totalled US$860 million ($1.1 billion) in 2026 thus far as the city-state’s safe-haven reputation and a low interest rate environment fuels investor interest.

This is already ahead of the full-year tally in 2025, and is on track to reach US$1.3 billion for the whole of 2026, said JLL on Nov 17 as it released its Hotel Investment Highlights Asia Pacific 2H 2026 report.

The gain reflects deal size rather than deal count, with three single-asset deals above $250 million anchoring the total, according to the real estate consultancy.

Large headline transactions announced this year have included the $500 million sale of the 575-room Crowne Plaza Changi Airport. The Robertson House by The Crest Collection, a 336-key luxury hotel along the Singapore River, also changed hands for $360 million , while the 272-room Orchid Hotel in Tanjong Pagar fetched $273 million .

Meanwhile, cross-border capital accounted for 54% of Singapore’s year-to-date transaction value, double the level in 2025.

Investor interest in the city-state’s hospitality sector is the strongest for “well-located assets with repositioning potential, co-living conversion opportunities, and leasehold properties offering attractive yield spreads”, JLL said.

At the same time, limited supply and robust demand continue to support fundamentals.

“The combination of a healthy financing environment should ensure that high-conviction capital will transact at scale,” said Tan Ling Wei, executive vice president of investment sales at JLL’s hotels and hospitality group, Singapore.

However, broader deal flow will depend on sellers showing greater pricing flexibility. “The persistent bid-ask spread remains the primary headwind for smaller assets, with owners holding firm on pricing and yield-sensitive buyers staying disciplined,” she added.

Singapore is also among the top five Asia Pacific (Apac) markets that hotel investors are targeting, alongside Japan, South Korea, Australia and India, going by JLL’s latest sentiment survey, which polled 120 hospitality owners and investors in September 2026.

The survey found that about 88% of investors favour traditional hotels, with a particular interest in upper-upscale properties.

For Apac overall, year-to-date hotel deal values have surged 50% y-o-y to US$12 billion through September 2026 — marking the region’s strongest performance for this period since 2019.

JLL now estimates that Apac could post a full-year transaction value of US$15 billion, as investor confidence firms up further in spite of geopolitical tensions and macroeconomic headwinds. It is up from the firm’s previous US$13.3 billion forecast published earlier in the year.

“The Apac hotel investment market has clearly entered a new phase of maturity and conviction,” said Nihat Ercan, Apac chief executive officer of JLL’s hotels and hospitality group.

He added that investors stayed in the market in 2026 and “capital is now more discerning”.

“Furthermore, with 58% of investors expecting cap rates to expand, buyers are putting conviction where consensus has yet to form: regional cities, repositioning and living conversions,” Ercan said.

Japan was again the region’s largest hotel investment market, accounting for 39% of total deal value at US$4.7 billion, followed by mainland China (15%) and Australia (11%).

Private companies were the most active investor type across Apac in the first three quarters of this year, representing 31% of total deal value. Next were investment managers and private-equity funds (19%) and listed companies (14%).

The region’s jump in investments has been underpinned by strong hotel trading fundamentals, with revenue per available room (RevPar) increasing 5% y-o-y between January and August 2026 amid sustained growth in average daily rates.

That said, the elevated geopolitical uncertainty remains one of the main risks in the market, as any material escalation could impact cross-border investor sentiment.

JLL also highlighted the continued volatility in interest rates across the region, with the cost of debt having increased for about 63% of investors this year.

Finally, another risk is the persistent bid-ask spread between buyers and sellers, which has stayed at 6% since last year. This could slow the pace of transactions if pricing expectations do not align, JLL noted.

title: Fewer shophouses sold this year, total deal value down 18%: Huttons estimates
article:
Singapore’s shophouse market is projected to close 2026 with a lower deal volume and value than last year, although it is likely to rebound in 2027, according to Huttons Asia.

The full-year transaction volume for 2026 is estimated at 75 units, down from 92 units, while total value may reach $675 million, declining 18% y-o-y from $823 million, Huttons noted in its outlook report on Nov 16.

Transaction volume and value of shophouses in 2026:

This came as investor sentiment was initially dampened by geopolitical uncertainties stemming from the US-Iran conflict in early 2026.

Buyer confidence then gradually returned to the supply-constrained segment of shophouses “as the market assessed the risks to be contained”, Huttons wrote.

Amid the uncertain environment, more than 60% of shophouses sold in the first quarter of this year were below $5 million — the highest proportion for that price range since 2Q2020.

Sentiment went on to improve in the subsequent quarters of the year, which led to a recovery in appetite for larger-quantum assets.

Retail investors have accounted for the majority of buyers in 2026 thus far, mainly targeting assets priced below $10 million and in Districts 7 and 8, which include Kampong Glam, Bugis, Rochor, Beach Road, Little India, Farrer Park, Serangoon Road and Jalan Besar .

In contrast, institutional property funds focused on investment-grade shophouses with value-add potential.

Districts 14 and 15 also continued to be popular among investors, Huttons said. Those districts span areas such as Geylang, Paya Lebar, Aljunied, Joo Chiat and Katong.

Five highest-priced shophouse transactions in 2026 to date:

Source: URA, news reports, Huttons Data Analytics (data downloaded as of Nov 12, 2026)

By price quantum, the largest shophouse deal for the year involved three adjoining freehold units along Lorong Liput in Holland Village , sold to TL Developments for $70 million .

In second place was Chinatown conserved shophouse trio The Platinum at 44, 46 and 48 Upper Cross Street, which changed hands at nearly $36.9 million based on an Oct 27 caveat.

That is below its latest guide price of $45 million when it was relaunched for sale in July this year . The Platinum was initially put on the market in July 2025 with a $55 million asking price. The properties have a 99-year lease that began in 2002.

Huttons also noted that many investors, looking for entry points into the market, are turning to 99-year leasehold shophouses, which offer a more accessible price tag.

At the same time, existing owners face little pressure to sell unless valuations meet their expectations, given the scarcity of the asset class.

Huttons noted that this shift is reflected in the larger proportion of 99-year leasehold properties sold this year, at an estimated 18% — up by five percentage points from last year.

Median rents and rental volume of shophouses:

Meanwhile, in the leasing market, shophouse rents have stayed largely flat in 2026, weighed down by persistent operating headwinds in the F&B sector.

Average rents of shophouses held steady at $6.50 psf per month over the year, unchanged from 2025.

Looking ahead, Huttons anticipates overall transaction activity bouncing back next year.

This is even as the prospect of rising interest rates could compress the spread between net yields and borrowing costs, and prompt some buyers to pivot towards lower-priced assets.

The property agency forecasts 2027’s sales volume to match 2023’s tally of 131 units. In particular, this will be buoyed by an upcoming portfolio sale of 50 conservation shophouses worth about $500 million to 8M Real Estate.

The Business Times (BT) reported earlier this month that the 50 shophouses — said to be individually held by separate groups of investors — are within the Tanjong Pagar Conservation Area , in areas such as Duxton Road , Duxton Hill, Tras Street , Craig Road and Neil Road .

The portfolio sale is expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027, according to BT.

title: Hilton's Apac hotel openings in 2027 to include first Waldorf Astoria in Tokyo and Sydney
article:
Hilton is set to expand its presence across Asia Pacific (Apac) in 2027.

The global hospitality company, which operates 28 hotel brands ranging from entry-level to luxury entities, will roll out new properties across countries including Australia, China, India, Japan, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam.

The properties span urban retreats to beachfront resorts and include brand debuts in multiple markets.

Key launches scheduled for 2027 include the first Waldorf Astoria properties in Japan and Australia.

The 197-key Waldorf Astoria Tokyo Nihonbashi will occupy nine floors of Tokyo Midtown Nihonbashi, a mixed-use development directly connected to Nihombashi Station.

Slated to be unveiled in autumn next year, it will include an indoor pool, luxury spa and restaurants. Waldorf Astoria will also operate branded residences at Tokyo Midtown Nihonbashi.

In Australia, Waldorf Astoria Sydney is scheduled for a 3Q2027 opening.

Located at Circular Quay, the hotel will offer panoramic views of the Sydney Opera House and Sydney Harbour Bridge. It will also feature a signature dining programme led by acclaimed Australian chef Curtis Stone.

Meanwhile, Motto by Hilton and LXR Hotels & Resorts will make their presence in Australia next year, with properties in the Sydney CBD and Gold Coast, respectively. The properties are targeted to welcome guests by the third and fourth quarters.

In Southeast Asia, Hilton will expand its Conrad brand with new properties in Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam.

In Malaysia, its 481-room Conrad Kuala Lumpur will be ready in the first 1Q2027. Located along Jalan Sultan Ismail, close to the Petronas Twin Towers and the Bukit Bintang area, it includes a panoramic rooftop restaurant and an infinity pool.

The 300-room Conrad Bangkok Sukhumvit Queen’s Park is also slated for a launch in the first quarter. It will be the second Conrad property in the Thai capital, following its inaugural hotel close to Lumpini Park that opened in 2003.

Meanwhile, the 208-key Conrad Phu Quoc — anticipated to make its debut in late 2027 — will mark the brand’s first hotel in Vietnam.

Hilton is also bringing its flagship Hilton Hotels & Resorts brand to Phu Quoc, with a 918-room property, also scheduled to be rolled out in late 2027.

Other Southeast Asia roll-outs include The Nautilus, Curio Collection by Hilton in Langkawi, Malaysia. The 249-room hotel near Cenang Beach is aiming to mark the brand’s presence on the island in 2Q2027.

Elsewhere, Hilton will introduce its Tapestry Collection in Maldives. The 75-key Coco De Mer Maldives will welcome guests in 2Q2027.

In China, Motto by Hilton Shanghai Wuliqiao will be launched in the second quarter. In India, Hilton will debut its Signia brand in Jaipur with a 289-room property in 4Q2027.

Separately, Hilton has also announced its first Tempo-branded property in Southeast Asia: a 164-key hotel located in Phuket, Thailand. The new-build hotel located in Bang Tao will be operated by Hilton in partnership with Thai company Sindhu Development Co. It is expected to open in 2030.

title: The Assembly Place appointed to manage Handy Road mixed-use property
article:
The Assembly Place has been appointed to manage and operate a standalone mixed-use property at 6 Handy Road, in the Orchard area.

In a Nov 17 announcement, the co-living operator said its subsidiary, TAP Co-Livings, has been appointed as property manager and operator for 6 Handy Road by an affiliate of ICHAM, a Singapore-based wealth and asset management firm.

Last month, The Assembly Place had announced it will invest up to $2.5 million in a living sector fund established by ICHAM, an affiliate of investment holding firm ICH Group. The fund has a target size of $300 million.

The Assembly Place will be appointed as property manager and operator of the fund’s property assets, aligning its interest with the fund’s investors while generating recurring property management and operating fee income.

The property at 6 Handy Road, named The Luxe , is a mixed-use development comprising 16 residential units and commercial spaces on the first and second floors. The 99-year leasehold development was completed in 2008.

The Assembly Place plans to transform the property into a serviced residence and co-living development with over 100 keys, subject to obtaining the relevant regulatory and planning approvals.

The property is a two-minute walk from the Dhoby Ghaut MRT interchange, which serves the North-South, North East and Circles lines. It is also a three-minute walk from Bencoolen MRT Station on the Downtown Line.

It is a short walk to nearby malls such as The Cathay and Plaza Singapura , along with other lifestyle amenities along the wider Orchard Road shopping belt.

"6 Handy Road offers a strong opportunity for us to unlock the potential of a strategically located property within Singapore’s prime retail district with its proximity to various MRT lines and educational institutions,” said Eugene Lim,  The Assembly Place’s executive director and CEO.

Vincent Toe, ICHAM’s investment manager, added that the property has “clear potential to be repositioned to enhance cash flow generation and unlock long-term value”.

title: W Singapore – Sentosa Cove introduces new wellness facilities through three partnerships
article:
2At W Singapore – Sentosa Cove , three brands — AiRe Wellness, L’évive Labs and Lume Red Light — have rolled out new recovery and wellness facilities.

The additions include a guided recovery centre, a wellness drinks bar and red light therapy equipment, alongside upgrades to the hotel's existing Away Spa.

AiRe Wellness has opened a recovery centre offering hyperbaric oxygen therapy, as well as red light therapy, compression recovery and body composition assessments.

Guests can also receive guidance from recovery coaches on sleep, nutrition, mobility, breathing exercises and stress management.

“We believe recovery deserves the same attention as performance,” says Derrick Seeto, founder of AiRe Wellness.

title: Renovating your HDB flat? Five security checks to make before works begin
article:
A few weeks after collecting the keys to our new four-room Build-To-Order (BTO) flat at Kovan Wellspring, messages about strangers entering units began appearing in our residents’ chat groups.

Then, in September, three middle-aged women walked into our flat without asking, while my husband and interior designer were farther inside. They said they wanted to see the place, and left after being questioned. Thankfully, nothing was taken or damaged.

Other residents have shared similar concerns in the estate chat, including an unknown visitor captured on CCTV inside a unit undergoing renovation. Another case even involved a cut lock and two missing shower heads.

Such incidents involving unauthorised entry, tampered locks and missing items have also been reported at newer HDB estates in Woodlands , Bidadari and Hougang , according to other news outlets.

For homeowners, the renovation period presents a degree of security risk — multiple contractors may need access to the flat, owners are not always on-site and high-value items such as fittings or appliances could be delivered when nobody is around.

This can be especially relevant for HDB flats, whether BTO or resale, as access to the block and common corridors is generally less restricted than at many private condos with gated access.

Here are five questions worth clarifying with your interior designer (ID) or contractors before and during renovation.

1. Who has access to your flat?

A renovation project can involve electricians, plumbers, carpenters, painters and other tradespeople arriving at different stages. Depending on how the project is managed, some may need a key or the code to a temporary lock.

Jeslyn Neo, interior designer at San Studio, says this makes it difficult for homeowners to know exactly who has entered the unit.

“During renovation, there are many different contractors coming in and out,” she says. “Homeowners may also not be there every day.”

Neo recommends limiting access to those who need it. If a combination lock is used, homeowners can change the code after a particular trade has completed its work.

Before each stage begins, homeowners should confirm with their ID who will receive the key or code, whether contractors are allowed to share it with

subcontractors, and who is responsible for overseeing access.

2. How is your flat secured while work is ongoing?

With workers coming and going throughout the renovation, homeowners should consider how to keep their flat secure while allowing contractors to move materials and equipment in and out.

“As much as possible, the gate should remain locked even when workers are inside,” suggests Neo. “If materials are being transported, it may make sense to leave the door open. But once that is done, workers should secure the unit again.”

Homeowners can also let the workers know what to do if they see an unfamiliar person trying to enter. Rather than assuming the visitor is another contractor or the owner’s guest, they can check with the ID or homeowner first.

A police crime advisory put up at Kovan Wellspring also advises homeowners to secure their gates and windows, and to avoid using number locks on the main door during renovation.

Instead, the advisory recommends closed-shackle locks, which leave less of the shackle exposed and therefore make it more difficult to cut or tamper with.

3. Can you monitor who enters the flat?

A CCTV surveillance camera or webcam can provide another layer of visibility, particularly for homeowners who cannot visit the site regularly. That said, this may not be practical at every stage of renovation. Power points may not be ready, while Wi-Fi is usually not installed yet, which can affect whether the camera can record continuously or be monitored remotely.

The police advisory recommends considering CCTV cameras and security alarms. The Singapore Police Force’s broader burglary advisory also suggests placing cameras near entry points and other vulnerable areas, and keeping them visible as a deterrent.

Neo says that where CCTV is feasible, the entrance is usually the most useful area to observe.

Homeowners should also check how footage is stored. Some cameras save recordings to a memory card inside the device, while others upload footage to cloud storage over the internet.

If Wi-Fi is not available yet, a camera with local memory-card storage may still be able to record, although homeowners would need physical access to the device to retrieve the footage.

It is also worth checking how much footage can be stored before older recordings might be automatically overwritten.

If CCTV is not practical, a simpler alternative could be to ask the ID or site supervisor for the day’s work schedule, so homeowners at least have an idea of what works would be taking place and which teams would be expected to enter the flat.

4. When should appliances and fittings be delivered?

As renovation progresses, sanitary fittings, lighting, appliances and other products may begin accumulating inside the flat before installation.

Where possible, Neo suggests arranging higher-value items to arrive closer to the date when they are slated to be installed. If an item has to be delivered earlier, it can be stored somewhere less accessible, such as a locked room.

The bomb shelter can also be used to keep items out of sight. However, bear in mind that according to HDB and SCDF regulations, the bomb shelter’s door cannot and should not be fitted with private padlocks, deadbolts or external key-latching locks.

Keeping a record of deliveries can help too.

“It is useful to take photos when higher-value items are delivered,” Neo says. “It gives the homeowner a simple record of what was received and where it was placed.”

Homeowners therefore ought to clarify who will receive and check each delivery, where the items will be stored and whether somebody is able to take photos of them.

5. Who secures the flat at the end of each workday?

Even if several groups of workers enter the unit during the day, there should be clarity over who is responsible for securing it once work stops.

Ask whether the ID, site supervisor or the worker who leaves last is expected to check the door, gate and windows before departing, and how the homeowner will know this has been done.

After the incident at our flat, this became part of the arrangement with our ID. Workers are reminded to keep the gate locked even when they are inside, and a photo is sent before they leave each day to show that the unit has been secured.

title: AEM: Earnings Beat, Bigger Backlog—and the “Razor Blades” Are Already Selling
article:
AEM’s latest results: stronger profits, a bigger order backlog and evidence that customers are upgrading equipment already installed.

At the 3Q results briefing, CEO Samer Kabbani said:

“This is an execution story that turns customer demand into financial performance."

CEO Samer Kabbani
3Q revenue reached S$204.9 million, up
110.7%
year-on-year and
57.2%
from the preceding quarter.
Profit before tax climbed to S$44 million, more than doubling sequentially.

A S$7.8 million tax credit boosted reported earnings.
Excluding it, earnings per share reached
10.7 cents
, compared with 5.1 cents in the second quarter.

Using AEM’s adjusted net margin, underlying quarterly profit works out to approximately
S$34.8 million
— about 34% above CGS International’s pre-results forecast of S$26 million.

The 9M2026 picture:

Test Cell Solutions is AEM’s main business segment for its semiconductor test equipment.

The “razor blades” are already selling

The most revealing exchange concerned AEM’s “razor-and-razorblade” model.
The idea is that AEM first sells the main test platform (‘the razor’), then earns follow-on sales from chip-specific modules and upgrades (‘the blades’).

These components adapt the testing machine to particular chips, allowing customers to change its capabilities without replacing the entire platform.

Sales of these “configurables and collaterals” reached
S$116.2 million
, representing 72.8% of Test Cell Solutions revenue.

But that is not AEM’s recurring-revenue percentage. Most current demand involves equipping newly installed systems.

Asked when customers would start upgrading existing equipment, Kabbani replied:

“It’s happening as we speak. Our configurables are a combination of brand-new products and upgrades.”

He added: “At the moment, we have a combination of both—we are refreshing while we’re deploying.”

Upgrades already contribute, although their share is undisclosed.
Customers reuse existing components whenever possible; bigger changes in chip power, size or testing requirements can trigger replacements.

This is repeat business linked to changing chip designs—not an automatic replacement cycle.

Better margins, without a promise

Adjusted net margin reached
17%
, up from 12.6% in the second quarter.

CFO Kwek You Cheer
CFO Kwek You Cheer
attributed this to both operating leverage and a better business mix: sales rose faster than costs, while Test Cell Solutions contributed more revenue.

CFO Kwek You Cheer

Asked whether customers bringing forward orders had helped profitability, Kabbani said there was no such unusual event explaining the gross-margin improvement.

Kwek nevertheless warned against extrapolating one quarter: “Yes, it may be strong, and it would take a couple of quarters to see how that will sustain.”

Bigger orders, clearer visibility

AEM raised full-year revenue guidance to
S$680 million–S$705 million
, from S$630 million–S$680 million. EPS guidance increased to
30–33 cents
, from 24.5–27.5 cents.

Kwek said that guidance excludes the tax credit that was booked in Q3 so as to focus on underlying profitability.

The midpoint earnings increase is about 21%, against roughly 6% for revenue. AEM expects to earn more from each dollar of sales.

The growth is coming from both major customers: its PC/foundry customer (Intel) and its fabless AI/HPC customer (widely speculated to be AMD) —a chip designer that outsources manufacturing. HPC stands for high-performance computing, including powerful processors used in AI servers and data centres.

Kabbani stressed that server processors, rather than ordinary laptops and desktops, drive the markets AEM primarily serves:

“Both customers are supply-constrained; they both have significant demand they can’t satisfy.”

AMPS, AEM’s platform for stress-testing advanced chips, had a backlog exceeding
S$450 million on 11 Nov
, versus over S$400 million in August.

Kwek supplied a delivery timetable: “We expect this to ship over the next two to two-and-a-half quarters.”

Kabbani clarified that the backlog covers AMPS alone, excluding AEM’s other platforms.

AEM Holdings' 3Q2026 Investor Update, 11 Nov 2026

The midpoint of revenue guidance increased
5.7%
, while the midpoint of EPS guidance increased
21.2%
, indicating stronger expected profitability.

Opportunities still need patience

Kabbani said AEM is pursuing large cloud operators’ custom-chip testing through ASE (a major company specialising in chip packaging and testing) and its PC/foundry partner.

“I think we’re progressing well on both fronts,” he said, while acknowledging long sales cycles.

Memory is behind schedule. Qualification of AEM’s Xact memory-testing handler is now projected to finish by 1H2027.

Cash deserves watching -- It fell to S$69 million while inventory and receivables increased. Dividends and buybacks accounted for S$10.8 million of outflows, so the decline was not entirely operational.

The takeaway: earnings and orders are delivering; upgrades are real.

AEM will provide 2027 revenue guidance in February.

title: S$10,000 in DBS Shares: How Much Dividend Income Could You Receive in 2027?
article:
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05) has long been a local favourite among Singapore investors seeking reliable dividend income.
The group’s popularity stems from its strong banking franchise, consistent profitability and track record of rewarding shareholders.
However, if you had S$10,000 to invest today, how much dividend income could DBS realistically generate in 2027?
In this article, we will examine the numbers and whether the bank’s current valuation makes it an attractive income investment.
How Many DBS Shares Can S$10,000 Buy?
On 6 November 2026, DBS shares closed at S$69.72.
With S$10,000, investors could purchase 140 shares.
This amounts to 14 board lots of 10 shares each, following Singapore Exchange’s reduction of DBS’s board lot size in October 2026.
At this price, the investment would cost S$9,760.80 before brokerage fees.
Assuming a S$10 brokerage fee, investors would have S$229.20 remaining.
Importantly, a higher share price means fewer shares for the same investment.
Had shares been bought at a lower price, the yield on cost would be higher, assuming dividends remain unchanged.
How Much Dividend Income Could DBS Pay in 2027?
DBS has progressively increased its ordinary dividends.
Recently, the bank declared S$0.66 per share for each quarter from 1Q2026 to 3Q2026.
Annualising these quarterly payments gives an ordinary dividend of S$2.64 per share.
Separately, DBS introduced a Capital Return dividend of S$0.15 per share quarterly in 2025, which management plans to maintain through 2027.
This represents another S$0.60 per share annually, although these additional dividends should not be treated as permanent recurring dividends beyond the announced period.

Under the base case, investors would receive S$369.60 in ordinary dividends and S$84 in Capital Return dividends, bringing total annual income to S$453.60.
This annual income works out to a monthly equivalent of approximately S$37.80.
The conservative scenario assumes ordinary dividends decline amid weaker earnings.
Meanwhile, the optimistic scenario assumes a further increase supported by stronger profitability.
Can DBS Sustain Its Dividend Payments?
DBS’s latest quarterly results showed
some pressure
, but overall earnings were resilient.
In the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), total income fell 1% year on year (YoY) to S$5.85 billion, while net profit declined 5% to S$2.81 billion.
The picture was slightly better when looking at the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), with net profit rising 2% YoY to S$8.82 billion.
For 9M2026, net interest income slipped 1% YoY to S$10.79 billion as lower Singapore interest rates were largely offset by loan growth and hedging.
In 3Q2026 alone, net interest income rose 4% YoY.
Meanwhile, its wealth management business continued to grow strongly.
For 9M2026, wealth management fees grew 24% YoY to S$2.69 billion, contributing to a 15% YoY increase in net
fee income
to S$4.37 billion.
In addition, DBS reported a Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio of 15.9% as at 20 September 2026.
With annualised earnings per share of S$4.15 for 9M2026 and an annualised ordinary dividend of S$2.64, DBS’s payout ratio works out to approximately 63.6%.
This provides some comfort for income investors, as loan growth and asset quality remained healthy in 9M2026.
However, lower interest rates, slower loan growth or higher credit costs could still put pressure on future earnings.
Is DBS Still Worth Buying for Dividend Income?
At S$69.72 per share, DBS’s annualised ordinary dividend of S$2.64 gives a yield of approximately 3.8%.
The inclusion of the planned Capital Return dividend would also increase the prospective 2027 yield to about 4.6%.
However, investors must recognise that this higher yield includes a time-limited payout.
At S$69.72 per share, DBS trades at around 2.85 times its net book value of S$24.47 per share as at 30 September 2026.
This multiple is known as the price-to-book (P/B) ratio.
The premium reflects DBS’s strong profitability, with return on equity reaching 17% for 9M2026.
However, its relatively high valuation also means that a slowdown in earnings growth could weigh on its share price.
Furthermore, investors should consider the risks of putting nearly all their S$10,000 into a single bank.
If investors spread their capital across different companies and sectors, it could help reduce their exposure to DBS’s performance.
Get Smart: How Much Can S$10,000 in DBS Really Earn?
Based on its current dividend payments and planned capital returns, having a S$10,000 investment in DBS could generate between S$420 and S$487 in dividend income in 2027.
The base case estimate of S$454 annually appears reasonable given DBS’s resilient earnings, capital position and current ordinary dividend level.
However, investors should note that the capital return dividend is only planned through 2027 and ordinary dividends are dependent on future profitability.
Ultimately, DBS is an appealing dividend stock, but its relatively high valuation means investors should weigh income received against potential capital losses.

reliable dividend

title: Get Smart: Nvidia Has Fallen 35%. Should You Buy, Hold or Sell?
article:
Singapore investors have been buying
Nvidia
(NASDAQ: NVDA) after its latest sell-off.
And it seems like they have been buying enthusiastically.
According to
The Business Times
, Nvidia orders on Syfe surged to around 13 times the daily average of the previous six weeks after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive last Thursday. Seventy per cent of Syfe clients who traded US stocks that day were trading Nvidia.
I understand the temptation.
I own Nvidia shares too.
The stock has fallen roughly 35% from its record high in early October. A company you already liked is suddenly available at a much lower price.
Surely that makes it a buying opportunity?
Maybe.
But before I ask whether I should buy more Nvidia, I think there is a harder question worth answering first.
Should I still own it at all?
What changed besides the share price?
Buying the dip sounds sensible because we tend to assume that the company we liked before is now simply cheaper.
Sometimes, that is exactly what has happened.
But not every falling share price is a bargain.
If something has changed about the business itself, then investors need to reassess what the company is worth and how much risk they are taking.
And quite a lot has changed at Nvidia.
Jensen Huang did not just occupy the CEO’s office. He co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it for 33 years.
He helped drive the launch of CUDA, pushed Nvidia towards artificial intelligence long before it became mainstream, managed some of its biggest customer relationships and represented the company in Washington on China export rules.
His sudden departure therefore creates genuine
key-person risk
.
Nvidia has appointed long-time CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor.
The question is not whether Nvidia can function without Jensen Huang. Of course it can.
The harder question is how much of the company’s extraordinary success came from decisions or actions that were uniquely his.
And it is likely that we won’t know the answer for some time.
The bigger risk may not be Jensen Huang
There is another issue that worries me more.
Nvidia’s board has launched an independent investigation following reports that Jensen Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence effort.
For investors, the important question is not the sensational part of the story.
It is whether the fallout ultimately affects Nvidia’s business.
In particular, could it result in tighter US controls over where Nvidia’s advanced chips can be sold?
That matters because China and export restrictions were already a major risk for the company before this happened.
If tighter rules apply broadly to American chipmakers, Nvidia could lose part of its addressable market.
But Nvidia-specific restrictions could be more damaging. Customers might then have more reason to move orders to competitors such as AMD.
In other words, this isn’t simply bad publicity.
There is a possible pathway from today’s headlines to Nvidia’s future revenue.
That deserves our attention.
But what hasn’t changed?
This is where things get more complicated.
Nvidia’s business
did not suddenly stop growing when Jensen Huang resigned.
Its most recent quarter generated US$96.2 billion in revenue, more than double the amount a year earlier.
Its near-term product roadmap was also developed while Jensen Huang was still running the company, and many customer orders have already been placed.
Nvidia also benefits from its CUDA software platform, which developers use to build AI applications. Because so much AI software has been developed around Nvidia’s technology, switching to competing chips isn’t always straightforward.
Meanwhile, the world’s biggest technology companies are still spending heavily on
AI infrastructure
.
These are reasons why I don’t think the answer is automatically “sell”.
But I don’t think it is automatically “buy the dip” either.
Buy, hold or sell?
For existing Nvidia shareholders, I think there are three reasonable questions to ask.
Would I buy more?
Perhaps, if I believe Nvidia’s long-term competitive advantages remain intact and the lower share price more than compensates me for the additional uncertainty.
Would I hold?
That may make sense if my original investment thesis remains intact, but I want to see how the leadership transition and investigations develop before committing more money.
Would I sell or trim?
I would have to consider this if Jensen Huang himself was a major reason I invested or if the regulatory risks have moved beyond my comfort level.
Or perhaps Nvidia has grown into such a large position that I am carrying more risk than I intended.
There isn’t one answer for every investor.
But there is one question all of us should be asking.
Get Smart: A cheaper stock isn’t necessarily a better bargain
When shares fall, it is tempting to focus on how much cheaper they have become.
But price is only one half of the equation.
If the risks surrounding a company have increased at the same time, then a lower price may simply reflect a different investment proposition.
Some might believe that a 35% decline has handed them an opportunity to buy more.
Maybe it has.
But for me, I want to answer a more important question first:
What has changed besides the price?

Here’s how each business is benefiting from the trend, and what its numbers tell dividend investors.
How is Micro-Mechanics riding the chip cycle?
Micro-Mechanics makes precision tools and parts used in semiconductor manufacturing.
For the first quarter of fiscal 2027 ended 30 September 2026 (1QFY2027), its Consumable Tools division contributed 75.8% of revenue through the sale of tools that reduce defects and improve yields in advanced chip packaging, assembly and testing.
1QFY2027 revenue rose 45.0% year on year (YoY) to S$24.2 million, an all-time quarterly high.
Net profit climbed 102.8% YoY to S$6.4 million, also a quarterly record, while gross margin widened to a 20-quarter high of 55.0%, from 51.5% a year ago.
The company links its outlook to wider industry demand, noting that global chip sales grew amid strong demand for AI, computing and memory, while it continues to see strong demand across its key markets.
Under a five-year strategy launched in FY2027, Micro-Mechanics aims to double revenue from FY2026 levels to at least S$150 million by FY2031.
Its balance sheet also stands out, with S$33.3 million in cash and no bank borrowings as at 30 September 2026.
Free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capital expenditure), however, slipped 10.6% YoY to S$3.7 million as capital expenditure rose to S$0.9 million from S$0.3 million.
Spending is set to climb further, with the company planning to invest S$12.0 million in FY2027 to expand its manufacturing footprint.
No dividend was declared for the quarter, in line with its practice of usually declaring dividends in the second and fourth quarters.
The company says its net cash position allows it to pay consistent dividends.
Can Digital Core REIT’s data centres grow its DPU?
Digital Core REIT
is a data centre real estate investment trust (REIT) sponsored by Digital Realty.
As at 30 September 2026, before a pending portfolio transaction, it owned 11 freehold data centres across the US, Canada, Germany and Japan.
It holds assets under management of US$1.9 billion.
Demand for data centres is showing up in rental rates, with new and renewal leases signed in the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026) achieving a cash rental reversion of 23%.
Management cites growth in AI workloads as a demand driver, but this has yet to translate into stronger income.
For 9M2026, revenue rose 1.6% YoY to US$134.5 million, but net property income (NPI) fell 4.3% to US$64.8 million, mainly due to the redevelopment of 8217 Linton Hall Road in Northern Virginia.
Distributable income to unitholders also slipped 1.1% YoY to US$34.8 million.
There could be an improvement ahead, as Linton Hall is now fully leased.
The lease is expected to start on 1 December 2026 and add US$18.1 million in annualised rent.
Management expects 2027 DPU of between US$0.0415 and US$0.0425, compared with a trailing 12-month distribution of US$0.0360, implying growth of roughly 15% to 18%.
Risks remain, though: in-service occupancy stood at 97.0%, while Los Angeles occupancy slipped to 84.1% from 85.6% as at 30 June 2026.
The pending portfolio transaction, which includes buying a 2.5% stake in a Singapore data centre, would also see the REIT enter Singapore.
The transaction would reduce aggregate leverage from 41.6% to 37.6% on a pro forma basis.
Where does Info-Tech Systems fit into the AI story?
Info-Tech Systems
is a software-as-a-service (SaaS) provider of cloud-based HR, accounting and customer relationship management (CRM) software, serving more than 28,000 businesses across five countries.
Its AI connection is through people rather than infrastructure, as its Info-Tech Academy runs AI-related training courses that have helped drive growth in its services business.
For 9M2026, revenue rose 20% YoY to S$42.6 million, while subscription revenue, which accounts for about three-quarters of the total, grew 11% to S$32.2 million.
Services revenue grew much faster, rising 82% YoY to S$8.6 million on demand for the Academy’s AI-related WSQ courses in Singapore.
Services now account for 20% of revenue, up from 13% a year ago.
Dividend investors, however, have less information to work with, as the update relied on unaudited management accounts and did not disclose profit or free cash flow.
Its CEO described a strong cash position and a debt-free balance sheet but gave no figures, and the update made no mention of dividends.
Management expects demand for Academy courses to normalise after an exceptional surge in 4Q2025, which came ahead of the expiry of a S$500 SkillsFuture Credit top-up.
This leaves a high base for the fourth quarter.
Get Smart: Buy the dividend, not the theme
All three companies point to AI as a source of demand, but that does not automatically make them good income investments.
Dividend investors need to look beyond the theme and check whether each business generates enough cash after funding its growth.
Does it have a track record of returning that cash to shareholders?
On the figures disclosed, Micro-Mechanics clears both checks.
Digital Core REIT is counting on a lease expected to start in December.
Info-Tech has yet to disclose enough information to assess its cash generation and dividend prospects.
Before buying any AI-linked stock for income, ask yourself one question: when the excitement fades, will this business still pay you?

topped the table, with its buyback accounting for 23.4% of the week’s total buyback value.
Its results for the quarter ended 30 September 2026 (3Q2026) provide useful context, with net fee income rising 19% year on year (YoY) to a record S$733 million on growth in wealth, cards and loan-related activities.
Gross customer loans also grew 6.0% YoY to S$372.3 billion.
Margins, however, moved in the opposite direction as the net interest margin narrowed to 1.68%, from 1.82% a year ago, mainly due to higher deposit costs.
Net profit attributable to shareholders came in at S$1.3 billion, up 182.2% YoY, although this increase came off a low base after UOB set aside S$1.4 billion in allowances, including pre-emptive provisions, a year earlier.
UOB did not declare a dividend alongside its 3Q2026 results, in line with its practice of paying dividends twice a year.
For 2027, the bank expects mid-single-digit loan growth and total credit costs of 25 to 30 basis points.
What sits behind Seatrium’s buyback?
Seatrium
bought the most shares of the three companies, while its buyback value ranked second for the week.
For the first half ended 30 June 2026 (1H2026), revenue rose 4.7% YoY to S$5.6 billion, with ship and rig building or conversion revenue climbing 17.5% to S$4.2 billion and more than offsetting a 29% decline in offshore platforms revenue.
Profit attributable to owners rose 158.3% YoY to S$372.9 million, but this figure includes a one-off S$171.7 million gain on the disposal of non-core assets.
Free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capital expenditure) was negative S$11.6 million, an improvement from negative S$31.9 million a year earlier.
Seatrium recognised revenue ahead of billings, lifting contract assets by S$1.6 billion to S$6.5 billion, while its balance sheet showed S$1.7 billion in cash against S$2.4 billion of debt, excluding lease liabilities, as at 30 June 2026.
Seatrium pays dividends once a year, so it declared no interim dividend for 1H2026.
Management guided that FY2026 net profit should come in materially higher than FY2025, helped by the one-off divestment gains.
How does SGX reward shareholders instead?
SGX
ranked 15th out of the 19 companies by buyback value, with dividends doing most of the work for its shareholders.
For the financial year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), net revenue grew 13.9% YoY to S$1.5 billion, while net profit rose 7.8% to S$698.4 million after a S$53.4 million goodwill impairment on its indices business.
Excluding that impairment and other adjustments, adjusted net profit rose 24.6% to S$759.5 million.
Free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capital expenditure) grew 2.0% to S$788.8 million.
SGX held S$1.8 billion in cash against S$628.2 million in borrowings, giving it a net cash position of about S$1.18 billion.
Its FY2026 dividends comprised:
Ordinary dividends: S$0.445 per share
One-off additional dividend: S$0.125 per share
Total: S$0.570 per share, up from S$0.375 a year earlier
Management guided for quarterly dividend increases of S$0.0025 per share through FY2028 and full repayment of debt in FY2027.
Get Smart: Follow the cash behind the buyback
A buyback shows that a company is willing to spend, but it does not tell you whether that spending can be repeated.
Before treating a buyback as a vote of confidence, look at where the money comes from and whether recurring profit and cash flow can support both dividends and share repurchases.
It is also worth stripping out one-off gains before judging the profit line, as Seatrium’s disposal gain illustrates.
For a bank like UOB, keep an eye on net profit and credit costs, while for SGX and Seatrium, free cash flow deserves closer attention because it is the lifeblood of dividends.
The next time a company tops the buyback table, ask yourself one question: will the cash that pays for it still be there next year?
