title: US homebuilder sentiment falls to fresh 14-year low on high rates
article:
(Nov 17): The mood among US homebuilders soured further this month, sliding to a fresh 14-year low as high mortgage rates deter would-be buyers and force builders to rely even more on costly incentives.

An overall market index from the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) and Wells Fargo decreased four points to 25 in November, the lowest since April 2012, according to figures released on Tuesday.

A reading below 50 indicates more builders see conditions as poor than good, and the gauge has remained below that threshold for more than two years.

The measure of present sales dropped six points to 28, also a 14-year low. Gauges of sales expectations and prospective buyer traffic both slid two points from a month earlier, NAHB data show.

“The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability,” NAHB chief economist Robert Dietz said in a statement.

The level of builder sentiment reflects an increasingly difficult market, including 30-year mortgage rates that remain well above 7%. The figures add to a steady drumbeat of disappointing news about the US housing market, including record low contract signings for previously owned homes and the weakest pace of closings since 2010.

See also: US October retail sales growth slows as car, furniture receipts slip

Nationwide, the NAHB survey showed that 46% of builders reported cutting prices this month, the largest share in the post-pandemic period. Some 68% reported using sales incentives.

DR Horton Inc has slowed its pace of housing starts to reduce the number of unsold homes. The biggest US builder also said on a recent earnings call that it expects to continue offering incentives to entice potential buyers.

Chief executive officer Paul Romanowski is not anticipating much relief in the way of lower home-financing costs.

See also: US colleges see further declines in international student enrollment

“Anticipating it to go down isn’t prudent at all,” Romanowski said on the call. “So as we look at our guide for the year and expect that we’re going to continue to see elevated rates, we’ll see how that progresses through the spring.”

The NAHB survey showed homebuilder sentiment fell in all four US regions to multiyear lows, with the South and West seeing their lowest levels in more than a decade.

On Wednesday, the federal government will issue its October housing starts report, while the National Association of Realtors will give an update on pending sales in the home resale market.

title: China warns US of retaliation over chip curbs, urges dialogue
article:
(Nov 17): China warned the US it would retaliate if Washington proceeds with curbs on remote access to advanced chips, while urging the Trump administration to resolve differences through dialogue.

The Ministry of Commerce in Beijing on Tuesday expressed “strong dissatisfaction and firm opposition” after the US unveiled sweeping new restrictions on China’s access to high-end artificial intelligence (AI) chips. Those curbs came days before President Xi Jinping is set to host his American counterpart for their third summit of the year.

“China hopes the US will work with us in the same direction and return to the right track of resolving differences through consultation and cooperation,” the ministry said in a statement. “If the US persists, China will take countermeasures to firmly safeguard its sovereignty, security and development interests.”

The measures run counter to understandings reached by the two countries’ leaders and threaten the stability of global semiconductor supply chains, the ministry added. A fragile trade truce that brought down sky-high tariffs between the two superpowers last year is currently set to expire in January.

Rules released on Monday by the US Commerce Department seek to prevent Chinese companies from renting Nvidia semiconductors outside the US and obtaining processors through Singapore and several other countries. They risk putting technology restrictions back at the centre of US-China tensions just as the leaders prepare to shore up their delicate detente.

The restrictions threaten to overshadow Xi’s meeting with Donald Trump this week on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen. Officials from the world’s biggest economies are also expected to hold their first AI dialogue over safety issues, a discussion that may now be coloured by their disagreement over hardware access.

See also: Nato turns to commercial rockets for greater space access

Beijing has been bracing for tougher US curbs since the downfall of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who had been the industry’s most prominent opponent of chip controls against China. Huang resigned last week amid revelations about extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former executive at a Singapore-based company under scrutiny over suspected chip smuggling and whom the US suspects of being a Chinese spy.

title: US October retail sales growth slows as car, furniture receipts slip
article:
(Nov 17): US retail sales growth moderated in October as a pullback in big ticket items like cars masked resilient demand for other goods.

The value of retail purchases, not adjusted for inflation, increased 0.2% after a gasoline-fuelled 0.8% advance in September Commerce Department data showed on Tuesday. But a gauge of underlying demand increased a stronger than expected 0.6%.

Seven of 13 categories posted increases, with higher outlays at nonstore retailers, health and personal care stores, gasoline stations and building materials merchants. Sales of furniture, motor vehicles and hobby supplies declined.

The report suggests uneven demand for merchandise at the start of the fourth quarter. Seasonal promotions in the month from companies like Amazon.com Inc may have supported sales, especially as consumers remain value conscious.

A stable job market alongside stock market gains have helped households weather widespread price increases, including for necessities like food and energy. Upcoming earnings calls from retailers like Walmart Inc will offer further insight into how Americans are prioritizing their discretionary funds this holiday season.

See also: US colleges see further declines in international student enrollment

“The consumer is in a fragile state,” said Kraft Heinz Co chief executive officer Steve Cahillane in its most recent earnings call. The company wants to limit price increases as much as possible “to meet the consumers where they are.”

Spending at restaurants and bars, the only service-sector category in the retail report, rose 0.2% — the weakest advance since March. Even so, the moderation follows strong increases across most of 2026.

So-called control-group sales, which feeds into the government’s calculation of goods spending for gross domestic product, rose by the most since August. The measure excludes food services, auto dealers, building materials stores and gasoline stations.

title: Disney profit beats with Marvel films powering streaming
article:
(Nov 17): Walt Disney Co reported sales and earnings that exceeded analysts’ expectations, with a particularly strong result in its streaming TV unit.

Operating income in the unit that includes the Disney+ and Hulu streaming services doubled to US$824 million in the fiscal fourth quarter, due to higher subscription and ad revenue, Disney said in a statement on Tuesday. Viewership of Marvel superhero-related programming more than doubled as fans caught up on the company’s catalog of Spider-Man and Avengers films, tied in part to theatrical releases from both this year,

Sales at the company overall rose 16% to US$25.9 billion, exceeding analysts’ projections for US$25.2 billion. Adjusted earnings of US$1.77 per share beat forecasts for US$1.66.

Josh D’Amaro took over as chief executive officer from Bob Iger in March and quickly embarked on a series of structural changes designed to streamline the sprawling entertainment giant and use Disney+ as the “front door” to connect sports, streaming, experiences and games. The company said on Tuesday it’s aiming for US$3 billion in annual expense savings by fiscal 2029.

Burbank, California-based Disney has already started several rounds of layoffs and could include thousands more.

The expected savings from job cuts are “meaningful” as the company seeks to sustain double-digit gains in adjusted earnings per share while continuing to invest in its highest-return businesses, Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Geetha Ranganathan wrote in a note before the results were released.

See also: US stocks fall before Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO

“The restructuring looks less like austerity and more like an effort to structurally lower the cost base, while protecting the earnings algorithm, she said.

Disney said in a letter to shareholders on Tuesday that it plans to plow much of the savings into its content budget. Cash spending on content will increase 9% in fiscal 2027 to US$26 billion, including an increased investment in sports rights and international programming. As content spending mounts, the company said it will no longer release operating income for the streaming business, including it as part of the overall entertainment division.

Disney shares slid about 2.2% in premarket trading in New York. Earnings expectations were already high leading into the results and the shares have gained about 19% since D’Amaro stepped into the CEO role.

See also: US stocks close lower after Nvidia spurs volatility in AI trade

Operating income at the company’s theme park unit rose 20% to US$2.25 billion, with attendance strength at Florida’s Walt Disney World and Disneyland Paris, as well as new cruise ships, powering the growth. Results were somewhat held back by weaker performance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai theme parks. Consumer product revenue rose 12% in the quarter, partly tied to new Avengers merchandise.

The sports division saw its profit climb 53% to US$1.39 billion, thanks to higher advertising revenue and subscriptions to the new ESPN streaming service. Viewership at the start of the season for NFL and college football reached historic highs, Disney said.

Fourth quarter and fiscal 2026 results overall were boosted by an additional 53rd week. The company is still projecting double-digit growth in earnings per share for the 2027 fiscal year. The annual dividend will climb 33% to US$2 a share.

The profit performance will be stacked in the first half of the year, driven by events such as the Dec 18 release of Avengers: Doomsday in theatres and February’s Super Bowl, which will air on ESPN, ABC and Disney+.

Disney expects flat operating income in the second half of the year at the resorts division, after seeing growth this year thanks to the new cruise ships, tariff refunds and the World of Frozen land opening at Disneyland Paris.

title: Enrichment class provider Tafa Holdings files draft prospectus for SGX IPO
article:
Despite the tepid scene for new listings, Tafa Holding plans to join the list of SGX IPOs this year.

The company, which provides enrichment classes, has filed its preliminary prospectus for an all-placement listing

Tafa Holding runs classes under different brands such as Tree Art and Futurum Academy, and has plans to develop more according to different curricculums.

The company now runs 16 Tree Art campuses and 6 Futurum Academy campuses in various locations across Singapore, while AK Robotics currently operates out of one campus in central Singapore.

In its latest full year ended Dec 31 2025, the company reported earnings of $102,000 on revenue of just over $14 million. In the year earlier FY2024, it made $105,000 and generated revenue of $12.3 million.

In the most recent half year ended June 30, it reported earnings of $2.1 million, reversing from a loss of $1.54 million in the year earlier. Revenue jumped from $5.2 million for 1HFY2025 to $9.46 million, with more students enrolled.

See also: Anthropic IPO set to cap year of record-breaking equity megadeals

The company is controlled by a married couple, Yang Cheng, who is the chairman, and his wife, Man Yi, who is the CEO. They each hold 40.5% of the shares.

title: Deluge secures $18.5 mil in new contracts, order book reaches $459.1 mil
article:
Deluge Corporation Limited (Deluge) announced that it has secured approximately $18.5 million in new contracts across both Singapore and Malaysia. With the latest contract win, Deluge’s outstanding order book has reached $459.1 million.

The new contracts secured span across infrastructure, marine and offshore, residential and industrial projects, which includes a data centre project in Penang, Malaysia.

In particular, Deluge states that the Penang data centre project is targeted for completion by March 31, 2027 and is expected to contribute positively to its financial performance for FY2027 ending March 31, which subjects to project progress and revenue recognition.

“Beyond growing our order book, our priority is to maintain strong execution while building a sustainable pipeline of opportunities to support long-term growth,” says Lee Wai Wah, executive director and CEO of Deluge.

Shares of Deluge closed 0.5 cents lower, or down 0.82% at 60.5 cents on Nov 17.

title: Geo Energy confirms no new mining directive received in latest clarification statement
article:
Geo Energy Resources, on Nov 17, confirms that its mining operations in Indonesia remain operational as usual and the group has not received any notice on new regulation, ministerial decree or implementing guidelines.

The latest clarification statement comes as recent media reports covers the remarks made by Indonesian President, Prabowo Subianto on Nov 14, regarding the government’s intention to secure a share of at least 70% of the benefits from all mining permits and if necessary, hold controlling stakes in mining assets.

Based on Geo Energy’s assessment of its existing fiscal contributions, the group has been contributing to the Indonesian government in excess of 70% of its profit through corporate income taxes, mining royalties and other applicable fees payable under the prevailing regulatory framework.

“Furthermore, the board also notes that President Prabowo had indicated that the relevant mechanisms had already been implemented, rather than referring to entirely new requirements yet to be introduced,” Geo Energy adds.

The group also confirms that its existing mining business permits (IUPs) remain valid and in effect.

“The IUPs for PT Tanah Bumbu Resources and PT Triaryani (TRA) are valid until Jan 10, 2028 and May 22, 2030 respectively, extendable twice by up to 10 years at the option of the group,” Geo Energy elaborates.

See also: Airwallex plans over $2 bil Singapore investment to support global growth

Nonetheless, Geo Energy states that it remains on track to achieve its coal volume target of at least 11.5 million tonnes for 2026. The group has attained coal production of 7.2 million tonnes in 9MFY2026.

Geo Energy says that it will make further announcements on this matter if and when there are further developments.

Shares of Geo Energy were last traded at 38 cents back on Nov 16 when the group calls for a trading halt.

title: UK backs push to explore global levies on climate polluters
article:
(Nov 17): The UK is among nations championing a push to add new levies on polluting sectors of the global economy and direct the proceeds to bolster funding to manage the impacts of climate change.

A declaration launched Tuesday at the COP31 climate talks acknowledged the potential for “small levies” to help mobilise climate finance for developing countries. Other nations backing the initiative include Spain, Kenya and Timor-Leste, the document said, confirming an earlier report by Bloomberg News.

The UK will continue to advance the proposals into 2027, when it will hold the presidency of the Group of 20 nations. Timor-Leste is chair of the Least Developed Countries negotiating bloc under the United Nations, which includes 44 economies.

Solidarity levies typically refer to surcharges on business class travel, financial transactions and fossil fuel production. The individual levies often raise only small amounts of revenue, though they are seen as an important tool to widen the pool of financing directed toward climate action.

“We recognise the potential of innovative approaches to complement existing sources of public and private finance,” the declaration said, urging a shift from “repeated and incremental crisis response to one of sustained and transformational resilience-building and proactive financing to match the scale of this challenge.”

Tuvalu, Vanuatu and South Sudan are also supporting the initiative, the declaration said.

See also: Strong on form, short on returns

The issue of securing adequate flows of finance to tackle global warming — and to adapt to its impacts — is the subject of fresh debate at the UN-convened COP31 climate summit in the coastal resort city of Antalya, Türkiye.

For adaptation alone, international public finance from developed to developing countries reached about US$32 billion in 2024 and compares to an estimated annual need of US$305 billion by 2035, according to the UN Environment Programme.

Developed countries, along with the European Union, have made clear at the Antalya talks that they will not commit to fresh climate finance commitments, meaning that other sources could have to make up the shortfall.

See also: EU close to deal to link UK carbon market after Brexit split

Earlier this month, Brazil published a road map on how to scale climate finance to US$1.3 trillion by 2035, which included the prospect of raising about US$129 billion a year through so-called solidarity levies.

“We welcome the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors and to mobilise more finance without adding to the sovereign debt burden,” the declaration said.

Almost US$200 million a year could be raised for climate finance by adding a US$60 to US$90 levy on premium airfares for flights arriving in 10 climate-vulnerable countries, the Global Solidarity Levies Task Force said in a report last week.

In an early draft of a COP31 decision text published Monday — one that is expected to be substantially revised in the coming days — the summit’s presidency included references to “innovative sources” of finance.

Last week at the talks, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called for additional taxes on fossil fuel companies to pay for the damage caused by climate change. A group of nine major producers had reported collective profits of US$95 billion in the last quarter — many multiples higher than funding available to respond to climate disasters, he said.

“Part of that should go into adaptation and loss and damage funds,” said Jennifer Morgan, a former German special envoy for climate.

title: Japan to launch natural disaster warning network across Asia
article:
(Nov 17): Japan will create a network across the Asia-Pacific region to promote development of early-warning systems aimed at bolstering protections against extreme weather events and natural disasters.

Gaps in capabilities such as remote sensing and cell phone alerts have been highlighted by recent events, including the devastating August floods near the Nepal-China border, which killed more than 1,400 people and wiped out towns, border posts and hydropower plants.

“The network will share knowledge and expertise in the introduction and operation of the early warning systems and promote effective deployment,” Japan’s Environment Minister Hiroyoshi Sasagawa said Tuesday (Nov 17) in a speech to the COP31 conference in Antalya, Türkiye.

Japan, which lies on an arc of volcanoes and fault lines surrounding the Pacific Basin known as the “Ring of Fire", has been a pioneer in earthquake early-warning systems and developing buildings designed to withstand powerful tremors.

The country also remains committed to supporting countries with climate finance, though it sees a need for other nations to contribute more, Sasagawa said.

“To meet the needs of countries requiring support, it is essential to broaden the contributor base to include countries capable of contributing and to expand various financial flows including private finance,” he said at the conference.

See also: Japan’s GPIF fund keeps quarterly asset allocation little changed

Developed economies have persistently called for the likes of China, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states to expand their climate finance contributions, while those nations argue that most responsibility should rest with countries that industrialised first.

title: US gas pump price hits lowest since March as oil supply recovers
article:
(Nov 17): US gasoline pump prices fell to the lowest since March following a broader decline in oil markets this month.

National regular unleaded gasoline dropped to an average of US$3.78 a gallon, according to the American Automobile Association. Global oil prices have fallen in recent weeks on increased flows from the Persian Gulf and indications from US President Donald Trump that he will hold off on renewed attacks against Iran.

While the move lower will be a welcome relief to US consumers, pump prices remain well above prewar levels.

title: Turkey fund assets shrink by US$54 bil amid manipulation probe
article:
(Nov 17): Türkiye’s asset-management industry shrank by the equivalent of US$54 billion in the two months through October as authorities investigated alleged market manipulation involving investment funds.

Assets under management fell about 17% to 13.14 trillion liras in October from 15.85 trillion liras in August, according to data from the Turkish Capital Markets Association.

The bulk of the contraction came in September, when the crisis erupted after Türkiye's capital-markets regulator ordered the liquidation of 131 funds managed by seven firms amid investigations into alleged manipulation of thinly traded stocks.

The seven managers’ combined assets plunged 85% to 281.7 billion liras in September, according to the data.

Türkiye's largest private banks meanwhile emerged from the turmoil with a bigger market share. The asset-management units of Isbank, Akbank, Garanti BBVA and Yapi Kredi now control 47.4% of the industry’s assets, up from 40.5% in August, as other managers bore the brunt of the losses.

The four firms collectively lost 188 billion liras over the two months, a decline of just 2.9%. Their combined assets rebounded by around 181 billion liras in October even as the broader industry continued to shrink.

See also: Dubai, Abu Dhabi investors’ options shrink on IPO slump, buyouts

Changes in assets under management reflect not only investor withdrawals but also fluctuations in market valuations and fund liquidations.

title: Nato turns to commercial rockets for greater space access
article:
(Nov 17): The North Atlantic Treaty Organization is contracting commercial rockets and spaceports to grow its satellite-launch network and help neutralise risks to the space systems on which it relies.

The alliance on Tuesday (Nov 17) launched its Starlift initiative, through which participating countries can secure slots on commercial rockets at spaceports across Nato countries and South Korea, deputy secretary general Radmila Shekerinska said at the opening of the Nato Edge technology conference in Izmir, Turkey.

The initiative is part of a Nato push to adopt more commercial technologies, with the alliance poised to offer more than US$3 billion in new private contracts in the next two years.

The expanded use of commercial launch providers and spaceports is intended to make Nato’s access to space more resilient and allow it to respond more quickly to threats, according to the alliance. Nato says its space systems — which support communications, navigation, intelligence and missile defence — face risks including cyberattacks and signal jamming.

Starlift will act as a launch brokerage platform, pooling military demand and matching it to commercial launch providers. It will also prepare and test procedures for short-notice launches, as might be needed during a crisis, according to Nato.

Ten members states — Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Turkey and the UK — along with South Korea have committed to financing Starlift through the Nato Support and Procurement Agency.

See also: Baidu’s Robin Li says AI needs monetisation to avoid bubble risk

Nato’s technology agency plans to offer about €2.7 billion in private contracts over the next two years, including to commercial space companies, Dylan Browne, general manager of the Nato Communications and Information Agency, said Monday. Other contracts will be for cloud, artificial intelligence, cyber, command-and-control and networks systems, Browne added.

“Nato must work with industry not only when a requirement has been finalised, but earlier,” Browne said. “We’ve got to work closer, with a clearer understanding of what the alliance needs next.”

Nato designated space as an operational domain in 2019 and has said attacks to, from or within space could lead to the invocation of its Article 5 collective-defence clause.

title: New UK relationship with Europe to take time, Burnham says
article:
(Nov 17): Prime Minister Andy Burnham said any major change in the UK’s relationship with the European Union (EU) would “take time” and wouldn’t be implemented until after the next election in Britain.

Burnham used a foreign policy speech for City of London leaders on Monday to set expectations for a summit with EU leaders on Friday in Brussels. While the prime minister said the meeting would usher in official talks about the future of ties to the continent, he said that any effort to significantly roll back the UK’s 2016 referendum to leave the bloc would have to wait.

“We will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship, recognising that both Britain and the EU are very different to what they were,” Burnham told the Lord Mayor’s annual white-tie banquet. “This will take time, and we will present those options and our assessment of them to inform decisions in the next Parliament.”

Debates about Britain’s relationship with Europe have consumed an increasing share of Burnham’s time since took he power in July and announced at the Labour Party’s annual conference plans to consider options for closer ties. While Burnham has said those options could include rejoining the EU, he has assumed a more cautious approach as Brexit advocates reinvigorate their anti-Europe campaigns and Cabinet ministers privately advocate caution, arguing that adopting European rules could risk recent gains in industries like banking and artificial intelligence (AI).

“The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain,” Burnham said on Monday. “Some sectors, like financial services and tech, have adapted well and are thriving. But others have suffered.”

On Friday, the UK and the EU are expected to seal deals to allow young people to study abroad, ease emissions trading and remove barriers to transporting agricultural and food items across borders. Burnham, a longtime supporter of the UK remaining in the EU, said he would advance legislation in Parliament next week to enact the deals.

See also: Burnham set to say Brexit has not worked

The speech reflects a Britain continuing to search for its place in the world in the decade since Brexit. Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, used appearances at the same event to argue that Britain wouldn’t be forced to choose between the US and Europe and needed to improve ties with China, despite its rivalry with the West.

In his own address, Burnham returned not only to Europe, but the Commonwealth of Nations, as platforms to maintain Britain’s influence on the world stage. He repeatedly offered a defense of liberalism, saying Britain would “lead with our values”, in a subtle critique of the “hard-headed realism” advocated by Starmer.

Burnham mentioned the UK’s most important security ally, the US, only once, and in passing, whereas Starmer’s had used his 2024 to defence of Britain’s continued relationship with an America that had just elected Donald Trump as the US president for a second time.

See also: UK's Burnham tries to hush down his own talk of rejoining EU

Burnham signalled continuity on Ukraine, reaffirming Starmer’s vow to maintain support for Kyiv “for as long as it takes”. The prime minister said he would join a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin on Thursday, affirming his predecessor’s approach to adapting to new questions about US security assurances.

He similarly affirmed support for the AI Security Institute, crediting then-Conservative prime minister Rishi Sunak with its establishment in 2023.

On Brexit, Burnham said the UK had to reconsider whether the exit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was “right for this moment, for our economy and for our security”. An analysis by Bloomberg Economics released in June found that leaving the EU had cost Britain between 2% and 4% of gross domestic product, and that various options short of full membership, such as rejoining a single markets for goods could bring in as much as 1.2 percentage points in recovered economic output.

“If we are going to be serious about growth, then we are going to have to have this conversation,” Burnham said, adding: “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”

title: Indosuez Wealth Management and INSEAD prepare heirs to better manage family business
article:
Indosuez Wealth Management (WM) has launched the Asian edition of Indosuez Academy, a programme which equips future business leaders with the skills to navigate the challenges and opportunities unique to family businesses.

Inaugurated in 2025 at the INSEAD Europe Campus in Fontainebleau, France, the academy’s first edition in Asia was held at INSEAD’s Asia campus in Singapore from Oct 26-29. Participants include children and grandchildren of the bank’s clients from around the world, including Asia Pacific, Middle East, Europe and America.

The programme, designed in collaboration with INSEAD, offers a unique platform for business heirs to expand their knowledge, connect with global peers, and embrace their future roles with clear purpose, says Indosuez deputy CEO Mathieu Ferragut. “For over 150 years, Indosuez has guided global families through complex cross-generational transitions,” he adds. “Bringing together a diverse 2026 cohort from multiple countries, this programme is designed to cultivate strong stewardship and entrepreneurial vision.”

The curriculum will equip participants with resilient leadership, crisis communication, and governance skills to balance legacy preservation with strategic growth and innovation.

Laurent Proutière, Indosuez WM CEO for Asia, says: “As Asia undergoes a massive intergenerational wealth transfer, the academy’s launch in our region is very timely. Business founders are increasingly focused on succession planning, and Indosuez is committed to supporting this next generation of leaders.”

Antoine Duvauchelle, programme director, INSEAD, believes that the programme provided a “safe space” for the participants to have their assumptions challenged, learn from each other and reflect on how they lead and make decisions. “It has been gratifying to observe how they are taking on board these learnings and evaluating what can be applied to their own business and family context as they prepare for the responsibilities that come with taking over the reins,” he concludes.

title: Shanghai Exchange intervenes after historic copper crunch
article:
(Nov 17): The Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE) has stepped in to try to ease an historic copper squeeze, as an acute shortage of available metal threatens to drain inventories.

Contracts for November delivery, which expired on Monday, soared to trade at a premium of over 14,000 yuan (US$2,100 or $2,707) a ton to contracts for delivery in December.

The dramatic spike on Monday came after on-warrant inventories had fallen to a level lower than open interest, raising the risk that more traders would request delivery than there was metal available to deliver.

To avoid that possibility, the SHFE pressured holders of long and short positions to settle them financially, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named as they weren’t authorised to speak publicly. While that achieved the desired effect of reducing open interest, it meant that short position holders were forced to buy back their positions, exacerbating the squeeze.

On-warrant stocks had fallen to just 2,270 tons last Friday, while open interest in the November contract stood at 4,810 lots, or 24,050 tons. SHFE had been encouraging holders of long positions to roll their positions rather than take delivery for several weeks, some of the people said.

See also: Aluminium squeeze intensifies with traders scrambling for metal

In early trading on Tuesday, the spread between December and January contracts widened, indicating that the squeeze may not be over.

Jia Zheng, a trading manager at Suzhou Chuangyuan Harmony-Win Capital Management Co, said that the tightness could persist until the end of the year. “Producers are holding back sales betting on spot premiums to continue rising, leaving buyers struggling,” she said.

See also: China’s US$17 bil crop pledge falters ahead of Trump-Xi summit

The squeeze is one of the most dramatic in the history of the copper market. The peak backwardation on the SHFE on Monday was twice that seen in a similar expiry squeeze on the London Metal Exchange (LME) in 2021, when the one-month backwardation flared out to as much as US$1,060 a ton.

It is also the latest in a series of short squeezes to hit metals markets, which have been left vulnerable by a drawdown in inventories caused by a variety of supply and trade upheavals ranging from US tariffs to the war in Iran. The LME copper market is also tight, while the LME aluminium market is in the grip of the biggest squeeze since the 1980s.

The Chinese copper market more broadly has tightened dramatically in recent weeks, with deliverable inventories falling to the lowest since 2023 and the premium for front-month contracts over later-dated months surging to the highest since 2005 — a condition known as backwardation that is indicative of short supply.

At the same time, physical premiums for copper — which are paid over and above the exchange price — have also jumped in China to trade at more than US$250 a ton, the highest in at least a decade. Bloomberg reported earlier that Trafigura Group had been buying large volumes of copper to boost sales into Asia, adding to a scramble for metal in the region.

The squeeze on supplies comes after copper flows were redirected away from China in the past two years, as traders rushed to ship metal to the US ahead of threatened tariffs. It also coincides with Asia Copper Week, as hundreds of miners and traders are descending on Shanghai to negotiate supply deals for the coming year with Chinese customers.

“Cathode is going to where the highest price is being paid, and that you know for now is Asia,” Nicholas Snowdon, Mercuria Energy Group’s head of metals and mining research, said at an industry conference in Shanghai on Tuesday. “Term premiums will in general be higher this year than last year, and the appetite for volume and long-term contract is much stronger than it was last year.”

title: France faces more strikes and protests over cost of living
article:
(Nov 17): French unions and student groups are planning another day of strikes and protests on Tuesday (Nov 17), testing the momentum of a movement that has brought repeated disruption in recent weeks.

Protesters are seeking to keep up pressure on the government after it offered concessions including a boost to the minimum wage and pledges to invest in education infrastructure.

“Our numbers and determination have forced the government to open its chequebook. Although their announcements are far short of our demands, we have made them react,” the student organization Coordination Nationale Lycéenne said in a statement calling for protests to continue.

The high school protests that began in September broadened into a backlash over rising living costs, with unions joining to demand higher wages in the public and private sectors. The grassroots Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018, has also participated.

Cost of living and inequality were front and centre at a presidential debate Monday night, when four candidates — Jean-Luc Mélenchon, Raphael Glucksmann, Bruno Retailleau and Gabriel Attal — sought to challenge the frontrunner Marine Le Pen.

See also: Merck KGaA lifts outlook again on life science strength

Polls show Le Pen, who leads the far-right National Rally party, will likely make it to the second-round runoff on May 2 with her far-left rival, Mélenchon. Le Pen is the favourite to succeed President Emmanuel Macron, polls show.

The candidates took aim at Le Pen in the debate, with Retailleau of the Republicans party, calling her multi-year budget proposal, which would cut €140 billion in public spending, a joke. Mélenchon has called for raising the minimum wage and instituting an inheritance tax.

A bolstered police presence at marches has largely avoided a repeat of Oct 17, when protests degenerated into rioting and looting across the country. Turnout has also faded at the most recent demonstrations.

See also: EU targets social media addiction and online ‘dark patterns’

The minority government is running out of margin to react to demands by protesters as it also faces a parliamentary showdown over the budget. Its capacity to respond is also restricted by a surge in borrowing costs, as the combination of political, social and fiscal difficulties sparked bond market selloffs.

The government has focused much of its response on proposals that have no direct impact on public finances, including raising a cap on regulated savings accounts and overhauling the procedure for university admissions. Still, the increase in the minimum wage announced last week will cost the state around an extra €1 billion as it also raises the lowest civil servant salaries.

“The problem is that with this government, it’s too little, too late,” Sophie Binet, the secretary general of the CGT union, said on Tuesday on RMC radio. “The only response we’ve gotten is a €5 monthly increase to the minimum wage. Frankly, that’s not nearly enough.”

title: Baidu’s Robin Li says AI needs monetisation to avoid bubble risk
article:
(Nov 17): Baidu Inc chief Robin Li sees an increasingly urgent need for better monetisation of artificial intelligence if heavy investments in the technology are to pay off.

Speaking at the Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen, Li summed up his view of the state of AI development as “very urgent” in a panel discussion with other executives. The Baidu chief executive officer has been underwhelmed by the pace of what he called, in English, “AI diffusion” across user-facing applications and hasn’t seen the tech helping boost sales and profit across companies.

Without a clear increase in revenue or profit for companies spending heavily on AI, “the common fear — that AI is merely a bubble — could well become a reality,” Li said on Tuesday.

Beijing-based Baidu is one of China’s earliest investors in AI, committing significant resources to developing technologies like self-driving software for years before OpenAI’s ChatGPT kickstarted a new wave in 2022.

Li said companies need organisational changes to better align with AI development, including breaking boundaries of occupational roles and teaching AI the valuable but unwritten rules within a company for how to get things done.

“I am still optimistic as AI is an inevitable trend,” he said. “It’s not that there’s a lack of AI demand, but rather it takes time for people to understand AI.”

See also: Pimco says AI bond spreads may tighten as data centre boom slows

Baidu on Monday posted its sixth straight quarterly revenue drop, underscoring the challenge for the internet pioneer in commercialising its AI ventures. Its shares have declined the most among leading internet names in China, in part because it has a less developed cloud infrastructure business than the likes of Tencent Holdings Ltd and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.

Still, Li said Monday that graphics card rentals — giving access to the essential accelerators for AI work — now contribute a larger share of the company’s profit.

title: New World just 1% of Henry Cheng’s US$27 bil fortune
article:
(Nov 17): New World Development Co’s plan to sell shares at a steep discount has roiled minority investors and threatens to dilute their ownership in the embattled Hong Kong developer. The founding Cheng family is taking a hit, too, but so far on a relatively smaller scale.

New World accounts for just 1% of billionaire Henry Cheng’s US$27.4 billion ($35.3 billion) net worth, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. As a result, the 41% plunge in New World’s stock on Monday won’t make a big dent in his fortune, amassed largely through the family’s jewelry business, dividends and other assets.

While the Chengs are risking their own money by funding the majority of the rights issue, the stock rout underscores how the real estate firm founded by Henry’s father Cheng Yu-tung more than 50 years ago has become a growing headache and ever smaller contributor to family assets. In one of the largest rights issues ever in Hong Kong, the indebted developer is offering US$3.2 billion in shares to existing shareholders at an 82% discount to where it finished trading last week.

New World is counting on its founding family’s support to persuade smaller investors to approve the deal, and to ensure continued backing from lenders. It’s the family’s most significant effort to rescue New World since it fell into financial distress, and its biggest capital injection to date. Their outsized participation followed pressure from banks for the billionaire Chengs to support the ailing developer before they would grant further loan extensions, people familiar with the matter have said.

An entity tied to the Cheng family, which controls the property firm, will inject as much as HK$18.7 billion (US$2.4 billion or $3.1 billion) into New World as part of the rights issue. That’s a drop in the bucket relative to Cheng’s fortune, which fell just US$281 million on Monday following the biggest decline in New World since the market crash of 1987.

See also: New World considering rights issue as Bain walks away — Bloomberg

“For the Chengs, they are buying in at a fraction of the book value,” said David Blennerhassett, an analyst at Ballingal Investment Advisors Ltd. “All stops are being pulled out to keep the company alive.”

New World didn’t immediately respond to a request for comments.

The fundraising plan is New World’s latest attempt to address its problems and reduce a pile of debt. The company, whose shares have fallen about 60% this year to a record low, is seeking to stabilise its financial position after years of liquidity strain caused by the property slump in Hong Kong and mainland China.

See also: Hong Kong listing proceeds hit six-year high, close to record

The rights issue also adds a wrinkle to an earlier deal with Hong Kong’s Airport Authority, which agreed to waive billions of dollars in rent that the company had committed to pay for its struggling 11 Skies project near the airport. The arrangement came with an option for the airport management body — wholly owned by the city’s government — to buy almost 30% of the developer’s shares at a then-steep discount.

Yet after Monday’s sell-off, the stock sits well below the price at which the option can be exercised. Based on the Nov 13 closing price, those options would have been sitting on a gain of HK$1.4 billion.

The rights issue might make the Airport Authority’s “share option worthless in the near to medium term”, and be unable to aid New World’s liquidity, Bloomberg Intelligence credit analyst Andrew Chan said in a note.

A representative of the Airport Authority said it would be inappropriate to comment on the potential dilution of the value of its share option.

New World still need a green light from minority investors to proceed with the rights issue. The plan faces a crucial vote by independent shareholders on Jan 5. Investors who don’t participate in the rights issue risk watering down their stakes by about 75%, the company said.

“It’s still at the discretion of shareholders to join, but we do not see many other viable options outside of joining,” Jeff Zhang, an analyst at Morningstar Inc, said of the rights issue. He sees the current market price implying a 60% chance the plan would go through.

title: Chinese AI stocks down as US chip curbs hit labs and hyperscalers
article:
(Nov 17): Chinese artificial-intelligence (AI) stocks tumbled on Tuesday after the US moved to further restrict access to advanced chips, with the country’s biggest hyperscalers and AI model developers among the hardest hit.

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd shares dropped as much as 5.6% in Hong Kong while Baidu Inc’s tumbled 6.6%, helping drag the Hang Seng Tech Index down 2.3%. AI model pure plays Minimax Group Inc and Z.AI Co, or Zhipu, fell more than 6% each, while robot maker Yushu Technology Co sank as much as 11% in Shanghai.

The broad sell-off underscores how tighter US restrictions threaten multiple layers of China’s AI industry, from cloud giants supplying computing power to model developers racing to catch up with US rivals. The proposed rules could raise the cost of accessing advanced compute and close off overseas routes Chinese firms have used to work around existing restrictions.

“We see this as a negative development for China’s AI cloud industry, as tighter access to advanced computing resources could constrain AI model training and slow cloud revenue growth,” Nomura Holdings Inc analysts Jialong Shi and Rachel Guo wrote in a note.

The draft regulation would require data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to obtain a US government license before exporting advanced chips to customers in those countries. That would go a step beyond existing restrictions that prevent Chinese tech firms from directly buying some of the most advanced US chips.

See also: China’s top AI firms limit cyber capabilities in latest models

The new rule was released days after Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s chief executive officer following his admission to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Tech investors remain on edge with key earnings also due this week from Nvidia as well as Alibaba and Tencent Holdings Ltd.

“The curbs add a concrete risk to revenues and access to computing capacity, but they are landing in a market already nervous about AI valuations, spending returns and Nvidia’s leadership outlook,” said Charu Chanana, the chief investment strategist of Saxo Markets. “This is a meaningful escalation.”

The fallout extended beyond China. Samsung Electronics Co fell as much as 3.3% and Advantest Corp slid 6.3%, extending losses among Asian technology hardware shares already under pressure from the turmoil surrounding Nvidia and persistent concerns over AI financing.

See also: China’s economy disappoints with stimulus yet to lift investment

“Tighter restrictions could raise concerns about slowing sales growth and may weigh on earnings in the short term” for Asian chip-related firms, said Hideyuki Ishiguro, the chief strategist of Nomura Asset Management. Some investors may also be selling holdings to raise cash ahead of the initial public offering of Anthropic PBC.

Southeast Asian stocks exposed to the AI build-out also came under pressure. Malaysia’s YTL Power International Bhd, which has benefited from expectations of surging electricity demand from data centres, slumped nearly 10%.

Chinese chipmakers were a notable exception, as investors bet tighter US restrictions will accelerate the shift toward home-grown technology. Hong Kong-listed shares of Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp climbed as much as 6.4% while Hua Hong Grace Semiconductor Ltd surged 12%.

title: Trump backs Huang comeback while Nvidia board seeks new CEO
article:
(Nov 17): US President Donald Trump supported calls from some Silicon Valley leaders for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia Corp’s chief executive officer, despite the chipmaker’s board moving forward with its search for a new chief executive officer.

“I would not mind that,” Trump told reporters on Monday at the White House before leaving for his trip to Asia, when asked about the possibility of Huang returning as the CEO. “A lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea.”

Nvidia’s board isn’t considering Huang’s return as it embarks on a search for a new CEO, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Nvidia fell 4.1% in New York trading on Monday, though the shares had briefly turned positive as Trump spoke.

Huang has discussed the possibility of returning to his position with his confidants, the Financial Times reported on Monday. A “war room” of Silicon Valley executives is also being organised to lobby for Huang and get the White House’s backing, the report said.

Trump’s position puts him at odds with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who called for a “dramatic shake-up” at Nvidia and an external search for new leadership. The president also played down concerns about the tech titan’s relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, saying he didn’t think that Huang’s actions jeopardised US national security.

See also: US, partners agree to safeguard key AI tech, infrastructure

“It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China,” the president said.

Trump also cast doubt on allegations that Alice Huang — a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International with whom Huang admitted having an affair — was indeed working for the Chinese government.

“Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” he said. “She may not be a spy.”

See also: Post-Jensen US chip curbs threaten Southeast Asia’s AI boom

Bessent has said that the US Commerce Department was responsible for Megaspeed not being added to the entity list that would have cut it off from sensitive US technology.

In a joint statement on Monday night, the Commerce and Justice Departments said that Commerce had begun probing Megaspeed “for potential export control violations” in 2024, and in May 2025 investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. A month later, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, according to the statement.

Based on the inquiry, “agents from the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang”, the departments said. The Justice Department then took over supervision of the case.

Justice and the “Bureau of Industry and Security will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred”, the two departments added in the statement.

Trump’s support for Huang reflects the close bond the two men have forged since the president’s return to power early last year. Huang has enjoyed the kind of access to the White House that few corporate leaders had, and the Nvidia chief seized on his proximity to Trump to lobby for looser restrictions on sales of Nvidia’s prized artificial intelligence (AI) chips to China.

Despite Trump’s dismissal of the security concerns surrounding Huang’s affair, Nvidia’s board is conducting an inquiry into the matter, as are US government agencies. For now, Nvidia says it has no reason to believe sensitive corporate or government information was exposed, but that investigation remains in its early stages.

Federal law enforcement authorities also have an espionage investigation underway, along with probes of possible chip smuggling involving Megaspeed. Key committees in Congress are kicking off their own national security reviews. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing, and Alice Huang is now in China, Bloomberg has reported.

Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter has agreed to testify before key House committees early next month.

“We look forward to meeting with the chairmen on Dec 2,” the company said in a statement.

The president’s openness to Huang’s return to the chipmaker added to a growing number of calls from Silicon Valley leaders and other investors for bringing him back as the CEO.

In a social media post, investment firms Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time” and the uncertainty created by his departure in urging the board to take a “slow, measured, and deliberate” approach to Nvidia’s future leadership.

That should include “the potential return of Jensen Huang”, Altimeter’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides’ Gavin Baker wrote in a letter to Nvidia’s board posted on X. SpaceX and Tesla Inc CEO Elon Musk, another Huang ally, has also voiced his support for a comeback.

Trump, who is travelling to the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen later this week for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ meeting, said he might raise allegations of Chinese spying on Nvidia with Xi Jinping when they meet on the summit’s sidelines. The president and his officials had earlier said he would not bring up the matter with his Chinese counterpart.

Beijing has denied the espionage claims and called them “purely a smear”.

title: Gold rises from 14-month low as dip buyers offset rate-hike bets
article:
(Nov 17): Gold edged higher — after its lowest close since September 2025 — as dip buyers brought some relief from stubborn US inflation and a selloff in technology stocks.

Bullion gained as much as 0.6% to near US$3,880 an ounce, erasing most of a loss from the previous session. The metal has been under pressure as expectations grow that the Federal Reserve will extend interest rate hikes into 2027. A recent rout in stocks related to the artificial intelligence trade has also pushed investors to offload holdings to cover losses. Silver has tracked the decline, also ending Monday at the lowest in more than a year.

Fed Bank of Cleveland president Beth Hammack said Monday she favours small and steady rate increases but that the central bank may need to consider larger moves if inflation worsens. Higher rates are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest.

“Precious metals remain skewed to the downside as further Fed tightening prices into the market,” TD Securities analysts including Ryan McKay wrote in a note, adding that gold was coming under more near-term selling pressure from traders at the Shanghai Futures Exchange.

However, both retail and institutional investors — convinced of the long-term bull case for gold — could be encouraged to resume buying now that bullion has crossed a key psychological threshold. “Below US$4,000, central banks that stepped back at elevated prices could return, providing structural demand,” said Yuxuan Tang, head of rates and foreign-exchange strategy at JPMorgan Private Bank.

This week, investors will be focused on minutes from the US central bank’s October meeting. In remarks Monday sketching out scenarios for the effects of AI, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh steered clear of offering any direct comment on monetary policy, in line with his stated preference not to provide near-term guidance on interest rates.

See also: Gold extends fall below US$4,000 as market watches Fed

Spot gold was 0.5% higher at US$3,875.15 an ounce at 1.08pm in Singapore. Silver rose 1.1% to US$47.54 an ounce, having tumbled 3.6% on Monday. Platinum and palladium also advanced. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, fell 0.1%.

title: Citi rules out major wealth acquisitions in hunt for US$5 tril
article:
(Nov 17): Citigroup Inc is pursuing US$5 trillion ($6.5 trillion) in wealth balances held by existing clients with rival firms, while ruling out major acquisitions, according to its wealth chief.

“We’re focused on organic growth,” Andy Sieg said in an interview in Shanghai. Chief executive officer Jane Fraser has been “extremely clear” over the past six months that the bank’s strategy centres “exclusively on organic growth”, he said.

Sieg’s remarks follow a report that Citigroup’s top executives were weighing the purchase of a major regional bank to bolster deposits. The New York-based lender oversees about US$1.4 trillion in client balances, leaving its wealth division trailing Wall Street peers such as Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan Chase & Co.

“We always think about different options,” Sieg said. “But we have just simplified the business dramatically over the last five years, and we feel like the footprint that we have today and the booking centres that we have today are the right ones for us.”

Fraser has spent the past several years streamlining the lender by cutting thousands of jobs and exiting international consumer businesses. The turnaround is gaining traction, with Citigroup recently posting its strongest third quarter in a decade. Sieg joined from Bank of America Corp. in 2023 to overhaul the wealth unit — a central pillar of Fraser’s push to lift returns.

See also: Banks need a better answer than keeping humans in every AI loop

In the third quarter, the bank attracted a record US$38 billion of net new investment assets globally. Sieg expects to continue delivering high single-digit organic growth in new flows.

To grow assets, the bank is looking to leverage off its investment bank, having introduced “partnership awards” to encourage collaboration between the investment bank and wealth. They were paid out for the first time this year.

It’s also using its retail footprint in the US, Hong Kong and Singapore to deepen relationships with its affluent clients, said Sieg.

See also: OCBC’s dividends could show the most growth in FY2026

The Asia Pacific wealth business generated revenue of US$2.58 billion in the first nine months of the year, up 13% from a year ago. It’s one of the fastest growing regions for the bank, said Sieg. It makes up about 27% of overall wealth revenue.

“We’re going to maintain discipline, but you are going to see steady growth in our banker headcount continuing in Asia,” said Sieg.

Sieg, who spent last week travelling across cities in China, including Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen, said that technological innovation in the world’s second largest economy is fuelling wealth creation and growth.

China’s push to collect taxes from the wealthy has stoked anxiety among the rich. The bank has held talks with Chinese clients and regulatory and tax considerations are discussed, said Sieg. Some clients have been affected by the changes but the bank hasn’t seen an overall impact on its flows across wealth, he said.

Citigroup is not advising clients to pull back on their allocation to equities given the strong momentum in US corporate earnings, according to Sieg. “We are still recommending large-cap, high-quality equity holdings,” he said.

The bank is advising clients to keep fixed income duration short and is talking to client more about owning gold as part of their portfolios, he said.

Sieg doesn’t see artificial intelligence (AI) meaning less hiring of wealth advisers for the bank, though he expects it to improve services and make advisers more productive.

“We are incredibly bullish on AI and what it’s going to mean,” he said. “And we are also hiring advisers at the same time.”

The bank has an AI-powered avatar called Citi Sky that’s now “in pilot” in the US and plans to unroll it in Asia, though he declined to give a specific date.

title: Aluminium squeeze intensifies with traders scrambling for metal
article:
(Nov 17): An aluminium supply squeeze is intensifying, with extreme tightness in near-term contracts leaving traders scrambling for metal.

The Tom/next spread on the London Metal Exchange, which represents the price to roll positions forward by one day, jumped to more than US$15 a tonne. Today is the last day that traders with short positions in the November contract can roll them over. Spot prices spiked to more than US$250 a tonne above benchmark three-month futures on Monday, another indicator of the dearth of supply in the market.

“There’s building potential for prompt spreads, front-end spreads to have further bouts of tightness,” Nicholas Snowdon, Mercuria Energy Group’s head of metals and mining research, said at an industry conference in Shanghai on Tuesday (Nov 17). “When I think about the next few weeks and months, it’s still a market that’s going to have very limited inventory cover.”

Aluminium stockpiles that back LME contracts have more than halved this year and are at the lowest level since 1990. A wave of new production is expected to push the broader market into surplus next year but much of that additional metal will not initially be deliverable on the LME, leaving exchange inventories vulnerable to further pinch points.

Global supply is set for its biggest year-on-year increase in three decades, Snowdon said, with output expected to grow about 6% next year against demand growth of roughly 2%.

title: China’s top AI firms limit cyber capabilities in latest models
article:
(Nov 17): China’s top artificial intelligence (AI) developers are releasing advanced models with reduced offensive cyber capabilities, stifling their ability to aid online attacks following a government proposal to ban such technology from being exported.

Recent models from Alibaba Group Holding Ltd, Tencent Holdings Ltd and Moonshot AI have featured scaled-down offensive abilities and improved defensive aptitude. Alibaba unveiled the latest edition of its flagship Qwen series without its weights, the internal settings that shape how a model responds, preventing users from downloading and customising the model’s full version.

So-called open-weight systems are attractive to hackers because they can run them locally and configure their settings. DeepSeek’s models have proved particularly popular, while Alibaba’s Qwen series has been ranked among the most downloaded open-weight model families in the world.

For months, US AI companies have also been restricting access to their most cyber-capable systems. Anthropic PBC has kept its Mythos Preview model out of general release, making it available to selected organisations for defensive security work.

Last month, researchers at CrowdStrike Holdings Inc said hackers used DeepSeek’s model to carry out attacks against organisations in 14 countries.

“The cyber ability of models, and soon the bio ability of the models, will reach a threshold where it’s actually possible to do harm,” said Yao Shunyu, Tencent’s chief AI scientist who previously worked for OpenAI, at an event this month in Hong Kong.

See also: China’s economy disappoints with stimulus yet to lift investment

Tencent reduced cyber functions from its Hy4 model before releasing it earlier this month. Moonshot took a similar approach with its Kimi K3.1 Pro model, while Z.AI carried out security reviews and alerted organisations to system vulnerabilities before making its GLM-5.3 system open-weight in August.

The moves follow a series of signals from China’s government about the risks posed by AI.

Last month, China’s Ministry of Commerce unveiled plans for an export ban on AI tools capable of attacking critical national infrastructure, attacking government networks or threatening military targets. Under the draft proposal, large language models deemed “world-leading” could also face restrictions on overseas deployment.

See also: China car output slows to four-year low as domestic demand drops

In early November, China’s top economic planner said it was accelerating the roll-out of new safety standards and ethical guidelines for AI developers. An official at the National Development and Reform Commission said there’s now a broad consensus about the opportunities and risks of AI, and that the country intends to embed security measures during the development process.

“China is trying to strike a balance between international commercialisation and strategic control of its AI technologies,” said Charles Li, the chief analyst of TeamT5, an organisation that tracks Asia-Pacific cyber activity. “As Chinese frontier models reportedly narrow the gap with their US counterparts in cybersecurity capabilities, Beijing increasingly views these capabilities as strategic assets that warrant tighter export controls.”

In the US, AI products were linked to a spate of autonomous cyberattacks in recent months, raising concerns about the technology’s ability to carry out offensive operations without human oversight.

Over the summer, American firms Anthropic PBC and OpenAI reported incidents in which their models eluded security controls and attacked third-party websites. The spate of incidents alarmed researchers and government leaders, prompting calls for more rigorous safety screening and more secure testing environments. In collaboration with the US government, Anthropic has allowed a select group of organisations to test the cyber abilities of its most advanced systems.

Chinese AI models have raised similar fears, with Moonshot’s Kimi K3 breaking out of a testing environment from the UK government’s AI Security Institute. Though the model did not try to breach other companies’ websites, as in some of the other episodes, the test showed it lacks cybersecurity controls, researchers said at the time.

Stripping cyber offence materials from training is a good way to make it harder for bad actors to use open-weight models to do harm, said Xiaojian Li, the founder of AI safety firm Fangcun AI.

“It’s a good balance between cost and effectiveness, but it’s not perfect,” he said. “There is no such method now that can completely eliminate models’ risk.”

title: South Korea to ground flights, delay trading for college exam
article:
(Nov 17): South Korea will temporarily suspend all aircraft takeoffs and landings and delay the opening of its stock market on Thursday as students sit for their high-stakes college entrance exams.

The flight restrictions will be in place for 35 minutes starting at 1.05pm local time to prevent noise disruptions while students take the English listening portion of the exam, the government said in a statement on Tuesday (Nov 17).

Aircraft that are already flying at that time must maintain an altitude of at least 3km (9,800 feet). Schedules for 130 flights — including 81 international and 49 domestic routes — will be adjusted, it said.

South Korea’s financial markets will also shift their schedules to help ease morning traffic congestion for test takers. The Korea Exchange will delay the start of trading by an hour to 10am and the stock market will close an hour later than normal.

The annual exam, called Suneung, is a gruelling one-day academic test that dictates which university a student will attend — a crucial step that ultimately shapes their future career prospects.

This year’s Suneung has emerged as a major test of public trust following a high-profile cheating scandal in South Korea’s national tax accountant qualification exams. The top scorer on that test said on Sunday that he used a miniature camera to photograph exam questions, sent them to an artificial intelligence system and checked the answers on a smartphone.

See also: China, Canada expand tariff relief in deepening trade thaw

In response, the government said it will form an intra-agency emergency task force to curb cheating involving AI technology and other outside assistance through stricter pre- and post-exam inspections. It’s also set to block public Wi-Fi access on exam day to prevent remote connections.

title: Pimco says AI bond spreads may tighten as data centre boom slows
article:
(Nov 17): Spreads on bonds financing the artificial intelligence build-out may tighten as a slowdown in data-centre construction curbs issuance, easing some of the pressure that a flood of AI-linked debt has put on credit markets, according to Pacific Investment Management Co (Pimco).

Investment-grade bonds backed by hyperscaler-leased data centres were trading about 146 basis points wider than comparable tenant debt as of Nov. 10, according to Pimco. The gap, near 180 basis points in late September, may narrow further as permitting constraints and higher costs delay construction and curb new supply, strategist Lotfi Karoui wrote in a note.

The call marks a shift from earlier concerns that AI borrowing was overwhelming investor demand and driving up financing costs. The Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections has since revived doubts over the payoff from massive AI investments. Consensus estimates put annual spending by Amazon.com Inc, Alphabet Inc, Meta Platforms Inc, Microsoft Corp and Oracle Corp above US$1.2 trillion in each of the next two years. Pimco expects some of that spending to be cut or pushed out.

“We expect a longer, and less linear, AI build-out rather than a materially smaller one,” Karoui wrote. That would spread financing needs over a longer period and ease near-term bond supply. Once recent volatility subsides, “we expect the underlying differentiation to reassert itself,” he said.

A slower build-out could keep computing capacity scarce, supporting utilisation and pricing at existing data centres, Karoui said. That may help hyperscaler-backed data-centre bonds outperform the technology companies’ senior unsecured debt, given their scarcity premium and wider spreads, he added.

Still, the opportunity won’t extend evenly across AI credit. Pimco is more cautious on leveraged infrastructure providers whose interest expenses, leases and chip-purchase commitments may persist even if construction setbacks delay the revenue needed to service them.
