title: China, Canada expand tariff relief in deepening trade thaw
article:
(Nov 17): China and Canada agreed to further tariff relief on agriculture and steel exports as President Xi Jinping and Prime Minister Mark Carney met in Shenzhen on Tuesday.

The pact builds on a trade truce signed in January between the two leaders, and forms a major part of Carney’s strategy to lessen Canada’s economic reliance on the US due to President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

The backbone of that initial deal saw China drop its tariffs on key Canadian agriculture exports such as canola meal, crabs and lobsters in exchange for Canada opening up its market to a capped number of Chinese-made electric vehicles.

The agreement announced Tuesday will see China extend tariff relief to a further C$400 million (US$280 million) worth of annual Canadian agriculture exports, including frozen pork cuts and a range of seafood products including certain shrimp, prawns, molluscs and halibut.

In tandem, Canada is expanding its list of tariff waivers for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products for which Canadian supply is either unavailable or insufficient.

Both sides have agreed to keep these measures in place until at least the end of 2028.

See also: India bank regulator reaffirms that Tata Sons must list shares — Bloomberg

“Canada and China have recalibrated our relationship to the benefit of both our citizens,” Carney said in a statement. He said his country is “diversifying our relationships abroad so that we have the freedom to live our lives as we choose.”

After their meeting, which took place ahead of an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, the leaders announced other measures to improve bilateral ties, including a large Canadian business trade mission to China in 2027, and new direct flights between Vancouver and Guangzhou.

See also: Former BOJ chief Kuroda sees chance of rate rising above neutral

“The improvement and development of China-Canada relations serve the interests of the peoples of both countries and also contribute to maintaining world peace, stability, and development and prosperity,” Xi said as he met Carney, adding that he looked forward to advancing “the new type of China-Canada strategic partnership.”

Carney hailed the “greater predictability and stability” that had come from a significant increase in the two countries’ exchanges.

The announcements didn’t include any significant changes to January’s auto pact, which allows up to 49,000 Chinese-made EVs into Canada at a low tariff of about 6%, exempting them from the 100% surtax Canada placed on Chinese EVs in 2024.

Although that quota is set to climb gradually, it appeared unlikely to be filled in its first year as Chinese automakers work to build up their Canadian retail presence and get certified by regulators.

According to a document released by Carney’s office Tuesday, 16,211 Chinese-made EVs have been imported into Canada since the quota took effect last March. A second Chinese automaker began exporting EVs to Canada in November, according to the document, which didn’t name the company.

The January deal also established a goal to “drive considerable new Chinese joint-venture investment” in automotive manufacturing in Canada within three years, but as of yet there has been nothing announced.

Ahead of his trip to China, Carney said Canada’s preference is still to integrate its auto manufacturing with the US market, but said his government will look to other countries — such as China — if Trump persists in putting high tariffs on Canadian car exports.

“Depending on where that settles — and it’s part of the trade negotiations — depending where that settles, there’ll be other options, European options, Asian options, of course,” Carney told reporters.

title: India bank regulator reaffirms that Tata Sons must list shares — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 17): India’s banking regulator has reiterated its stance that Tata Sons Pvt Ltd needs to list its shares to comply with local rules, in the latest blow to its controlling shareholder.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in a Nov 16 letter said that Tata Sons must follow all rules applicable to so-called upper-layer non-bank financial companies, including the listing requirement, according to people familiar with the matter. The letter was in response to the company seeking guidance on regulatory compliance, the people said, asking not to be named as the information is not public.

The letter doesn’t impose a fresh deadline or announce enforcement action, but confirms that there aren’t many options available to Tata Trusts, which owns about two-thirds of Tata Sons, the holding company that in turn controls the Tata Group. Led by patriarch Noel Tata, the Trusts wants Tata Sons to remain privately controlled — a stance that has stoked a broader power struggle between Noel and the Tata Sons board, which is willing to comply with the RBI rules.

Spokespeople for Tata Sons, Tata Trusts and the RBI had no comment. Local media including the Hindu Businessline reported on the letter Monday night.

Noel Tata warned over the weekend that a listing could undermine the group’s distinctive ownership model, allowing profit to “take precedence over philanthropy.”

RBI had rejected in September Tata Sons application to surrender its shadow lender tag in a bid to avoid listing. Tata Sons remains classified as an upper-layer non bank financial company — a designation that receives stricter regulatory requirements.

See also: Former BOJ chief Kuroda sees chance of rate rising above neutral

One of India’s oldest and most influential conglomerates that was founded nearly 160 years ago, Tata’s businesses span brands such as Jaguar Land Rover, Air India, Taj Hotels and Tetley tea. Its more recent projects include India’s first chip making facility and the local manufacturing of iPhones, making the group crucial to India’s high-end technology manufacturing ambitions.

title: China’s US$17 bil crop pledge falters ahead of Trump-Xi summit
article:
(Nov 17): China looks unlikely to fulfill a pledge to buy billions of dollars in US farm products in 2026 as the leaders of the two nations prepare for their third meeting this year.

President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are set to have talks this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen. The two sides agreed in September to lower tariffs on a slew of farm products. But nearly two months later, those cuts are still pending — and Trump’s bargaining position is expected to be weakened by Republicans’ midterm setbacks and Nvidia Corp.’s scandal.

Those issues, plus the war in Iran, are likely to take precedence at this week’s talks. Even as China closes in on a target to buy 25 million tonnes in US soybeans this year, the industry is pessimistic that a separate commitment to purchase an additional US$17 billion in American farm products will be met.

“I wish it would happen, but I think it’s pretty low,” AgResource Co analyst Ben Buckner said of the chances. “I would not be counting on China to buy corn or wheat from the US in the next 30 days.”

The US$17 billion pledge could get an extended timeline. But the lack of progress so far has been a disappointment for American farmers who, after being stuck in a yearslong slump, have lost some faith in US-China trade and had looked to the agreement as a way to regain stability in the market.

See also: Wheat falls on optimism about Black Sea talks, Argentine supply

While a failure to meet the target isn’t expected to derail wider trade relations, it could make it difficult for weak grain prices to recover. The Bloomberg Grains Spot Subindex is hovering near the lowest level since July, while input costs have soared with the Iran conflict, driving up fuel and fertilizer prices for farmers. With a record soybean harvest and bumper corn crop, a rebound increasingly hinges on demand.

A strengthening US dollar combined with a weaker Brazilian real and Russian ruble are also making American goods more expensive versus rivals.

See also: Copper sinks to four-month low on tech rout, China growth woes

“We will be the seller of last resort,” said Mike Zuzolo, analyst at Global Commodity Analytics and Consulting in Kansas.

China dominates global soybean imports and remains a large grain buyer, although a slowing economy has trimmed its purchases from peaks seen just a few years earlier. Weak prices for hogs — the main industry driving feed imports — leaves little incentive for the country to buy higher-priced supplies from the US.

Instead, China has been diversifying purchases across other markets, recently turning to France and Argentina for wheat and corn and Brazil for distillers dried grains and sorghum. Even as state-owned importers make steady purchases of US soybeans, tariffs are deterring private traders from joining the fray — a move that could accelerate purchases and widen demand to other crops.

“China has already demonstrated through soybean purchases by state importers that it is willing to pay above-market prices for US agricultural products when broader trade considerations are at play,” said Vladimir Zinkovski, head of Asia-Pacific crops research at S&P Global Energy. “Private importers, however, are unlikely to contribute significantly toward the US$17 billion target while current tariffs make US products commercially uncompetitive.”

Beijing never formally confirmed the US$17 billion deal announced by the White House in May, and it’s unclear exactly what it includes. The US said the dollar target is prorated for 2026, without specifying for how much or when the clock started.

AgResource estimates China has purchased all but about four million tonnes of a separate pledge to buy 25 million tonnes of US soybeans. But buying of other agricultural goods has been minimal. Through September, China’s purchases of US corn and wheat stood at a fraction of those seen prior to 2025, US Department of Agriculture data shows. No American corn or wheat are on the books for China in the 2026-27 season.

Successive record domestic corn harvests in China, alongside ample supplies of sorghum and barley, are limiting the commercial incentive for imports of the grain, Zinkovski said.

The National Corn Growers Association said China’s tepid interest in US farm products outside of soybeans is tempering expectations for demand from the country under the US$17 billion pledge.

“While we would be hopeful to see corn included in China’s target, due to the uncertainty around the terms, I do not think the market is pricing in an expectation for large corn purchases as of now,” Gretchen Kuck, an economist with the association, said in an email.

Beef offers another example of the gap between improved market access and actual trade. China renewed permits for hundreds of American beef plants in May, but shipments have barely recovered as surging US prices and tepid Chinese demand curbed purchases.

Still, while reaching the US$17 billion goal appears difficult and unlikely, any momentum on tariffs or non-soybean purchases would be beneficial, said Darin Friedrichs, co-founder of research firm Sitonia Consulting Co.

“Until now, there hasn’t been much movement outside of soybeans,” he said. “If there are reciprocal tariff reductions and increase in purchases of US grains, that would be positive for the US-China relationship, even if it is below the goal.”

During the first meeting of a new trade council on Friday, the two nations discussed a US$30 billion for US$30 billion reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement and agricultural trade — moves that could lead to the final implementation of the duties cut and boost Chinese purchases of other US farm products.

China’s commerce ministry has signalled an openness to boosting US agricultural purchases provided the two sides implement a deal to reduce reciprocal tariffs.

“The fact that they’re publicly saying ‘drop that tariff and we’ll do something’ is a good sign,” said Randy Place, senior grains analyst at the Hightower Report.

title: Former BOJ chief Kuroda sees chance of rate rising above neutral
article:
(Nov 17): Former Bank of Japan governor Haruhiko Kuroda flagged the possibility that persistent inflation risks might prompt authorities to raise the benchmark interest rate above the so-called neutral rate, where policy is deemed to be neither stimulative nor restrictive.

“It all depends on inflation,” Kuroda said in an interview with Bloomberg on Monday. “If inflation becomes more serious, then rate hikes will naturally have to accelerate as well, and rates may even have to rise above the neutral rate.”

Kuroda pointed to inflationary pressure stemming from US President Donald Trump’s war with Iran, which is raising costs for Japan because of its reliance on imports of oil, raw materials and food.

With the BOJ widely expected to raise rates next month, how high the policy rate might ultimately rise in this cycle has become a primary focus for investors. The median economist estimate is 1.75%, or essentially two more hikes, while some see it reaching as high as 2.5%.

Kuroda spoke roughly two weeks after the BOJ board led by his successor, Kazuo Ueda, reached a milestone by asserting that underlying inflation was consistent with the BOJ’s target for the first time since the goal was set in 2013. Kuroda said it was a favorable development, but the bank’s job isn’t finished.

Handpicked by then-prime minister Shinzo Abe in 2013, Kuroda presided over a decade of aggressive monetary easing that pushed the boundaries of conventional central banking and became a central pillar of Abenomics. He stepped down in April 2023 after two terms, making him the longest-serving governor in the BOJ’s history.

See also: Indonesia’s Prabowo apologizes to Singapore, Malaysia for haze

The former chief stressed that inflation would determine the BOJ’s future course. The BOJ’s price outlook is 2.5% for this fiscal year, but the average has been about 1.7% in actual data through September. The average monthly gain would need to sharply rise to about 3.3% in the next six months for the projection to be realised.

The interview took place hours after government data showed Japan’s economy contracted in the three months through September, with consumer spending declining partly due to unusually bad weather during the period.

Kuroda played down concerns about the contraction and said the weakness is probably “temporary.”

See also: ByteDance plans US$6 bil buyback at US$400 bil valuation — Bloomberg

A former Finance Ministry official, Kuroda also spoke as lawmakers debate Takaichi’s plan to cut the sales tax on food for two years starting in April. Takaichi has said households need support against inflation while critics doubt its effectiveness and question how to fund the measure.

The tax cut measures are expected to add around ¥10 trillion (US$62.7 billion) to the economy. That fiscal boost is likely to complicate the BOJ’s task as the economy is already running at capacity with strong employment — the jobless rate is a mere 2.4%, the former governor said.

“I don’t see the point. If you cut taxes under those circumstances, it’s obviously not going to raise the growth rate — it’s going to push up prices,” Kuroda said. “And if that happens, the BOJ will have no choice but to keep raising interest rates.”

One of the most controversial policies Kuroda deployed was a negative interest rate of -0.1% in 2016. In his book published last month, he revealed that at the time he thought it would be difficult to cut rates any further, even though the bank repeatedly pledged to do so if deemed necessary.

“Financial institutions may not have been able to stomach any further” given their inability to impose negative rates on depositors, Kuroda said. “Among central bankers it was a shared view that it can’t go deeper and deeper.”

title: New US export controls on Singapore, Malaysia for advanced chips to take effect Nov 19
article:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 17): A licence will be required to export, re-export, or transfer advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, or Brazil, according to the US Department of Commerce.

Effective Nov 19, the US' new rules aim to prevent certain foreign actors from using advanced, US technology-based computing power to undermine US national security and foreign policy interests.

Data centres, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in US-embargoed destinations, categorised under Group D:5, or Macau.

Country Group D:5 comprises US arms-embargoed destinations—some subject to embargoes aligned with UN sanctions, others designated unilaterally under US policy.

The department said the licence requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat.

See also: Don’t rule out Korea’s memory giants just yet: Goldman Sachs

"The licence requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met."

"Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR (interim final rule) and will consider a range of consequences for such countries," The US Department of Commerce said in a statement on Monday.

This development comes amid recent regulatory scrutiny over chip supply chains.

Malaysian authorities, including the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti) and the police, have been investigating Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd — a tenant at local data centres linked to Singapore-based Megaspeed — over US allegations of illicit procurement and potential re-export or diversion of advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence (AI) chips to China.

The IFR tightens the presumptions front-end fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips, narrowing the routes to overcome them for designers based in destinations subject to 'super intelligence' (SI) chip licensing. SI is a term for AI used by the Trump administration.

"This change gives the US government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries."

The IFR formally rescinds the Biden-era AI diffusion rule, which was never enforced, formalising the rescission that the US Bureau of Industry and Security announced in May 2025, said the regulator.

title: JPMorgan says 'technical issue' affecting customers resolved
article:
(Nov 17): JPMorgan Chase & Co, the largest US bank, said it fixed a “technical issue” that had caused customers’ transactions to take longer to process on Monday.

The disruption was related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems, the bank said that morning. Despite the challenges, customers still had access to their accounts and funds, and the issue wasn’t related to cybersecurity, the bank said.

By Monday evening in New York, a bank spokesperson confirmed that transactions were being processed normally again.

Tech challenges have been plaguing US companies and entities in recent weeks. Microsoft Corp faced one of its longest outages last week, with disruptions to Outlook, Teams and the Copilot artificial intelligence (AI) tool. US airlines were hit by one of the longest nationwide shutdowns in decades, with the Federal Aviation Administration saying the ground stop was tied to a router located near El Dorado, Arkansas.

Downdetector had earlier logged reports of disruption on Monday with JPMorgan. Other financial firms also saw a spike on Downdetector including Bank of America Corp and Wells Fargo & Co. Zelle, the payments system overseen by early warning services and owned by banks, was also among the apps listed as customers flagged problems.

JPMorgan said that other banks may have been impacted “only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us”.

See also: OxPay readies payments system in Bhutan; plods towards 2030 growth targets

A Wells Fargo spokesperson had no immediate comments. A Zelle spokesperson said its system wasn’t down and had been operating as it should. A Bank of America spokesperson said its systems had been operating normally.

JPMorgan shares fell 2.3% to US$338.21 ($436.11) on Monday, narrowing this year’s gain to nearly 5%. Bank of America was down 1.8%, while Wells Fargo dropped 1.4%.

Spokespeople for the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corp didn’t immediately respond to requests for comments. A spokesperson for the US Federal Reserve had no immediate comments.

title: Asia data centre hotbed hit by US chip curbs as Trump visits
article:
(Nov 17): US President Donald Trump is targeting Southeast Asia in Washington’s rush to tighten China’s access to the world’s most advanced chips, with his administration announcing new rules just before he travels to the region.

Data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will need a US government licence to purchase advanced AI chips from Nvidia Corp and other American manufacturers, according to an interim rule released Monday by the Commerce Department.

The region has seen a boom in data centres housing the semiconductors needed to train and develop artificial intelligence models. Some of that demand has come remotely from firms based in China including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd and Bytedance Ltd, whose access to the most-advanced chips Washington wants to block.

“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries,” the department said Monday in a statement.

Those four Southeast Asian nations, along with Brazil, also “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the advanced semiconductors that Washington has sought to deny Beijing.

See also: Singapore wealth fund, Saudi Telecom bid for UK’s Pure Data Centres stake — Bloomberg

In a statement, Singapore’s ministries of trade and digital development said the government was studying “this new measure carefully” and engaging with companies to understand its potential impact on their businesses. Brazil’s government said that it was “closely monitoring any developments” related to the rule and declined to offer an assessment of its impact.

Indonesia’s Government Communication Agency said officials were reviewing the measure and seeking industry input on any impact on operations and investment. It added that the government is working on a strategic trade management framework to “facilitate legitimate trade while reducing the risk that dual-use goods and technologies are diverted or misused.”

The other countries didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment sent outside normal business hours overnight. Nvidia also didn’t respond to a request for comment.

See also: Malaysian data centre loan syndication delayed in rare deal pause

Efforts to tighten US export controls on advanced chips have gained steam in Washington days after the resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive officer following his admission to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International whom the US suspects of being a Chinese spy.

In addition to the remote access rule unveiled by Commerce, US lawmakers are weighing a series of measures that would put additional curbs on sales of AI chips and further limit China’s access to sophisticated chipmaking machinery from ASML Holding NV. The measures would be attached to annual defense legislation that must pass before the end of the year.

New restrictions “would pose a major headwind to data centre investments in those countries going forward,” said Robert Walker, an economist in the Indo-Pacific Development Centre at the Lowy Institute in Australia, adding that “Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, to varying degrees, are most exposed to these risks.”

The debate in Washington over reviewing rules restricting remote access have been ongoing for months, particularly over the summer after China’s Moonshot AI released a model that scored nearly as high on benchmark tests as those from American rivals Anthropic PBC and OpenAI.

But the espionage scandal involving Jensen Huang accelerated the move and gave administration hawks leverage to force the Commerce Department to act.

Chinese companies still rely heavily on Nvidia processors to train cutting-edge models while domestic chipmakers play catch-up. At least 30% of China’s advanced AI computing power is forecast to come from renting overseas data centres and smuggling in Southeast Asia in 2027, according to previous estimates by the Institute for Progress, a Washington-based think tank.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The new rules — laid out in a 132-page document — were announced just as Trump left Washington for the region, with a first stop in Manila on Tuesday to meet leaders from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

“It’s going to make a very uncomfortable meeting,” said Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore. Given the timing of the announcement “that’s going to get mighty awkward.”

Trump heads next to Shenzhen, China, where he will meet leader Xi Jinping.

Also, travelling with Trump are Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who have sparred over Lutnick’s handling of US export control programs.

The announcement also comes as the US seeks to bolster cooperation with allies on advanced technology and infrastructure, part of its so-called Pax Silica initiative to compete with Beijing. The US and nine partners, including Singapore, agreed over the weekend to establish a framework for the protection of critical goods, software, knowledge materials, and components essential to AI supply chains.

The pact targets those items “whose theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage,” the US State Department said in a statement.

Cloud computing demand from Chinese firms has been a key driver of Southeast Asia’s data centre boom, but it can be hard to pin down the arrangements. Nvidia chip buyers are reluctant to disclose the identities of their Chinese clients, while those firms often take steps to distance themselves from the rental setup, even while it was allowed.

Alibaba, for example, accessed Nvidia chips located in Malaysia through Singapore-based Megaspeed.

But the agreement isn’t direct: Alibaba used a Singaporean shell controlled by an entity in the Cayman Islands, of which the Chinese tech giant is the ultimate holding company, according to documents reviewed by Bloomberg News.

The new Commerce Department rule will likely complicate such arrangements, according to Elms.

“That window just closed quite a bit and might be shut entirely to the certainty that you can have the current configuration of data centres, with the current list of companies that are using or renting space in the data centers,” she said.

Megaspeed has been under US investigation for possible export control violations over allegations the company illegally diverted AI chips to China. The company has denied any wrongdoing, while Alice Huang is now in China, Bloomberg has reported.

The global AI boom has also boosted several Asian economies that supply the hardware for data centers, with robust exports helping counter the hit from higher energy prices because of the Iran war.

While new US restrictions would likely impose a higher risk premium for some investments in Southeast Asia and dampen the data center business model, “the region’s place in the semiconductor supply chain is more secure,” said Lowy’s Walker. “Exports to the US are booming to basically supply the inputs that US data centres need.”

title: Simba plans board changes as spectrum breaches go uncontested
article:
Simba Telecom plans changes to its board after declining to contest unauthorised spectrum use and other breaches raised by Singapore’s telecommunications regulator.

Richard Tan will resign as a director of Simba and new directors will be appointed, subject to regulatory approval, says its parent company Tuas Limited in a Nov 17 filing to the Australian Securities Exchange. Simba is a wholly owned subsidiary of Tuas.

The operator responded on Nov 16 to the show cause notice it received from Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) on Oct 23.

It does not contest unauthorised use of the 2100 megahertz spectrum band for 4G, the 2340–2360 MHz band or 5G indoor radio access network equipment, in breach of its licences. It also does not contest breaching a document production order.

The company has explained to IMDA the circumstances surrounding the unauthorised spectrum use and outlined remediation steps it has put in place to seek to prevent a recurrence. The regulatory review remains pending.

“As the matter remains under consideration by the IMDA and no findings have been made or confirmed, Tuas does not intend to provide further comment on the matters raised in this announcement,” says the company.

title: Asian stocks to fall ahead of Nvidia, Anthropic
article:
(Nov 17) : Stocks in Asia looked set to decline, tracking losses on Wall Street as investors remained wary of the AI trade ahead of Nvidia Corp.’s high-stakes earnings and Anthropic PBC’s expected market debut.

Equity-index futures for Australia, Japan and South Korea all pointed lower after the S&P 500 fell 1.9% and the Nasdaq 100 slid 2.7%, both declining for a third straight session. A gauge of chipmakers sank 5.3%. The tech rout spurred demand for defensive assets, with Treasuries rising as oil prices dropped. The dollar edged higher.

Adding to pressure on tech shares, the US moved to curb Chinese companies’ remote access to advanced AI chips and servers. The Financial Times reported Sunday that Washington and its allies agreed to protect AI technologies and supply chains seen as vulnerable to China.

The selloff raises the stakes for two key tests of investor appetite for AI this week. Nvidia’s results on Tuesday will offer a read on demand for chips and the fallout from Jensen Huang’s exit, while Anthropic’s expected listing later this week will gauge whether investors are still willing to put fresh money behind the sector.

“There’s been a great deal of noise in the market lately,” said Chris Larkin at E*Trade from Morgan Stanley. “Stocks weathered last week’s Nvidia volatility, but earnings and a high-profile IPO mean this week will likely continue to revolve around tech sentiment.”

Nvidia is coming off its worst week since April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs upended global markets. Its shares fell 4.1% on Monday, helping drag down the broader Magnificent Seven.

See also: Stocks fall before Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO

Attention is also turning to whether Huang could return. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for a “dramatic” leadership shakeup, while Huang’s allies have pushed for his comeback, with the FT reporting discussions around that prospect.

Trump backed calls Monday for Huang to be reinstated and downplayed national security concerns about the ousted executive’s relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. CNBC, however, reported that Nvidia’s board isn’t considering bringing Huang back, citing a person familiar with the matter.

Anthropic’s listing, meanwhile, has drawn demand for about seven times the shares available, according to people familiar with the matter. Bankers expect to price the IPO on Wednesday, with trading set to begin Thursday in what could be the biggest first-time share sale ever.

See also: Asian stocks brace for AI pressure, data dump

The debut has taken on greater significance following the turmoil at Nvidia, offering another test of enthusiasm for AI companies and putting added attention on Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei as a prominent advocate for the industry.

“A successful IPO is important for Anthropic, and also for the entire AI sector,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, adding that financing from Nvidia to the company and other AI firms is likely to receive greater scrutiny following Huang’s exit.

Beyond technology, investors are weighing the US rates outlook after Federal Reserve officials signaled another increase is likely in December. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favors small, steady hikes, while Governor Christopher Waller has previously raised the possibility of a half-point move if inflation pressures worsen. Futures are pricing a December hike and another likely increase in January.

Elsewhere, oil fell as ample physical supplies outweighed the risk of Middle East disruptions, extending a two-week slide as Trump has appeared reluctant to escalate attacks on Iran following the Democrats’ midterm sweep.

“The prospect of a growing supply surplus appears to carry more weight than the risk of another disruption, leaving crude vulnerable to further selling unless tensions translate into actual supply losses,” said Ole Sloth Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank AS.

title: US stocks fall before Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO
article:
(Nov 17): A selloff in technology stocks carried into a new week as Wall Street traders geared up for Nvidia Corp’s high-stakes earnings and Anthropic PBC’s expected market debut in the coming days.

Chipmakers got hit again, with a key industry gauge dropping 5%. The Nasdaq 100 fell 2%. Traders will also scrutinise Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh’s remarks on Monday, with bonds edging up. Oil fell.

Nvidia remains a focal point after Jensen Huang’s departure. President Donald Trump supported calls for his reinstatement as the firm’s chief and downplayed national security concerns about the ousted executive’s relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

With increased scrutiny over semiconductor exports after an alleged espionage scandal involving Nvidia, the US Commerce Department moved to limit several countries from providing Chinese companies remote access to advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips and servers.

Meantime, Anthropic PBC’s debut this week will not only put pressure on chief executive officer Dario Amodei to fill the void that Huang left as the leading pitchman for technology. It also will require the firm to show that the AI gold rush has matured beyond the picks-and-shovels phase.

See also: US stocks close lower after Nvidia spurs volatility in AI trade

“There’s been a great deal of noise in the market lately,” said Chris Larkin at E*Trade from Morgan Stanley. “Stocks weathered last week’s Nvidia volatility, but earnings and a high-profile IPO mean this week will likely continue to revolve around tech sentiment.”

The AI lab is targeting a US$1.4 trillion valuation in its first-time share sale, below the US$2 trillion floated months ago, but well above US$1.1 trillion that some on Wall Street suggested in the depths of the recent selloff in tech stocks.

See also: US stocks bounce as Nvidia rout spurs gains elsewhere

Bank of America Corp CEO Brian Moynihan said deals are getting postponed into 2027, with investors pointing to Anthropic’s expected blockbuster initial public offering (IPO) crowding out smaller companies.

Capital-markets activity by the end of the year “will be up a chunk, but it’s been very bumpy,” Moynihan said in a Bloomberg Television interview Monday, adding that the pipeline remains full nevertheless. “Deals are getting pushed into early next year.”
